#4867. Toyota’s EV sales more than doubled in a year, but gas cars are getting crushed in China

Toyota’s EV sales have jumped 127% through September, but that isn’t telling the whole story. Slumping demand for gas and hybrid cars in China has pushed global sales lower for three months in a row.

Including Lexus, Toyota sold 309,766 battery electric vehicles (BEVs) globally through the first nine months of 2026, up 127.4% from the same period last year.

Except for January (+87.5%), Toyota’s EV sales have more than doubled every month this year compared with 2025.

The higher demand comes after Toyota and Lexus launched updated versions of their first-gen electric SUVs, the bZ4X (now the bZ in the US) and the RZ.

Toyota has added several new electric models, including the C-HR+ (C-HR in the US), bZ4X Touring (bZ Woodland in the US), and Urban Cruiser, while Lexus now offers the ES EV. Both brands will introduce a three-row electric SUV, which is expected to go on sale over the next few months.

According to data from Cleantechnica, the Toyota bZ4X became the 20th best-selling EV worldwide through August, with nearly 100,000 units sold.

While its EVs are catching on, Toyota Motor’s global sales fell for the third straight month in September.

Toyota sold 860,107 vehicles in September, down 2.2% from the previous year. The company said that although overall demand remained steady, sales in China fell, leading to lower overall sales than last year.

Through September, Toyota sold 7.51 million vehicles globally, down 3.4%. In China, Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20%, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales.

Toyota said the overall market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” resulting in lower sales.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Toyota sells several electric vehicles through its two joint ventures (GAC Toyota and FAW Toyota) in China, including the bZ3, bZ3X, bZ5, and bZ7.

After the US, China is Toyota’s second-largest market. Through September, Toyota has now sold more vehicles in its home market of Japan (1.19 million) than in China.

To turn things around and compete with companies like BYD, Toyota, like many major OEMs nowadays, is increasingly adopting more Chinese EV tech and manufacturing practices.

Nikkei reported in August that Toyota plans to build a new Lexus electric SUV in China, rather than in Japan as it has traditionally. Production is expected to begin at Lexus’ new manufacturing plant in Shanghai next fall.

Toyota's EV sales still represent less than 3% of its overall sales. This is the real news.

BTW, Toyota's European sales got hit in a similar way. They are up 0,7% YoY but that's compared to a rising overall market of 5,7%. This lead to it's market share shrinking.

The new Lexus EV will use advanced manufacturing methods, including gigacasting, to cut costs and speed up production.

Toyota isn’t the only legacy automaker struggling to keep pace in China’s fast-moving automotive market.

Volkswagen Group CFO and COO, Arno Antilitz, admitted the company “must act quickly and decisively” after reporting third-quarter sales in China dropped 38% to 405,800 units on Thursday. The company also plans to use technology developed in China for its next-gen EVs, which it will sell overseas.

#4866. Michael Strahan Shares the Words That Helped His Daughter Through Brain Cancer Treatment

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Michael Strahan appeared in commercials for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, delivering a message he never imagined would become so personal: “No parent should have to hear that their child has cancer.”

But in 2023, the beloved TV host and former NFL player faced that reality when his daughter, Isabella, was diagnosed with brain cancer at 19 years old.

“[That] line that I used to deliver, usually at the end of the commercial…here I am actually filling that line in my life in real time,” Strahan told Healthline.

Strahan believes his longtime connection with St. Jude was more than a coincidence. After years of advocating for families affected by childhood cancer, he found himself on the other side of that experience.

“When I needed that family…they were there for me,” he said. “I’m just appreciative, and I think things come back to you; give out good, good comes back.”

In October 2023, Isabella began experiencing vomiting, headaches, and balance issues during her freshman year at the University of Southern California (USC). Tests revealed that she had medulloblastoma, a fast-growing cancerous brain tumor located in the cerebellum. She underwent emergency brain surgery, radiation therapy, and four rounds of chemotherapy.

While medulloblastoma typically occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 9, it can also affect young adults like Isabella.

“[The] biology in adolescents and young adults can differ meaningfully from pediatric cases, requiring specialized expertise at centers of excellence for this disease,” Arnab Chakravarti, MD, director of the Brain Tumor Program at The Ohio State University, told Healthline.

Medulloblastoma is sometimes confused with glioblastoma, the most common type of malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma is particularly aggressive, with a median overall survival of just 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.

However, Chakravarti explained that medulloblastoma has a significantly higher cure rate than glioblastoma.

“[This is] a point of genuine hope that deserves to be communicated clearly,” he said.

Radiation therapy is a cornerstone of medulloblastoma treatment. Isabella received proton therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

“For medulloblastoma, this physical precision is transformative,” Chakravarti said. “Proton craniospinal irradiation dramatically reduces [collateral] exposure — preserving cochlear function and hearing, reducing cardiovascular risk, protecting the thyroid, and most critically, sparing developing brain tissue in ways that translate into measurably better neurocognitive outcomes years after treatment.”

He added that multiple prospective studies have shown that children and young adults treated with proton craniospinal irradiation experience less cognitive decline and better quality of life compared to those treated with conventional radiation.

Today, Isabella is back at USC, embracing the everyday routines she once had to put on hold.

“I am back at USC, so…it’s been great, in the midst of exams, so it’s a little stressful, but I actually [am] inviting the stress in because at one point I didn’t have exams, so I’m happy to be back,” Isabella told Healthline.

Along with attending classes, Isabella is enjoying activities such as working out and cooking. She continues to undergo MRI scans of her head and spine every three months, but said that after another year, the scans will become less frequent, occurring every six months.

“But really…I don’t have a lot of doctor’s appointments,” she said.

“It feels like a brand-new life, but it’s a good one. And that’s wonderful,” Isabella said.

Isabella said her family’s support played an important role in helping her through cancer treatment. Spending so much time together in the hospital brought them closer as they watched movies and played cards and board games to pass the time.

“[It] really, really bonds you to people, and just having my dad and my whole family there was something that [you] can’t beat,” she told Healthline.

Michael said that despite the difficult circumstances, he cherishes the time he spent with his daughter. Before her diagnosis, Isabella was a typical teenager who spent much of her time at school or with friends.

“They say you spend the most time with your kid for the first few years of their life, and then once school starts, you don’t get a chance to spend as much time as you would like with them,” he said.

While Michael said he and Isabella already had a close relationship, her diagnosis brought the family even closer and helped them reflect on what mattered most.

“[What] was really important was family, and relationships, and the love that you have for each other, and the support you have to give each other,” he said. “I think that our relationship now is better than ever.”

Today, Michael makes an effort to visit Isabella at USC whenever he’s in Los Angeles during the NFL season.

“Some weekends she [has time for me]. Some she doesn’t,” he said. “But just to have that relationship with your child, where they want to hang out with you, is a good feeling, and that’s the relationship that we have.”

Michael and Isabella are sharing their story to raise awareness about brain cancer and offer hope to other families facing similar challenges.

They recently participated in a fireside chat in New York City hosted by Real Chemistry and SMAC, where they discussed their family’s experience navigating Isabella’s diagnosis, mental health, caregiving, and the impact of sharing their story.

Throughout her treatment, Isabella also documented her experience through a series of YouTube vlogs and the ABC primetime documentary, “Life Interrupted: Isabella Strahan’s Fight to Beat Cancer.”

For Michael, helping others is a value he learned from his parents. He recalled how his father used his transportation business in Germany to support people in need after retiring from the military.

“[He] would take donations, and use his money and his trucks, and drive stuff to Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, and drop it off there at local churches and the shelters for people, who he had no connection with,” said Michael. “So for me, I think I do what I feel is on my heart and what’s important to me.”

For parents caring for children with cancer, Michael emphasized that it’s OK to feel overwhelmed or emotional. He encouraged them to show their children love and support while helping them maintain hope for the future.

“I think positivity is the main thing because it was so tough on her at the time when she was [saying], ‘I can’t do it. I can’t do this. I can’t do that,’” said Michael.

Michael said he made a conscious effort to replace words like “can’t” and “if” with “when” while encouraging Isabella during treatment.

“Anytime she got down on herself, I’d say, ‘when you go back to college, when you do this, when you do that,’” said Michael. “And I just think the positive attitude and the love that you can give and the confidence that you can display towards your loved one [or] your child who’s going through something like this is the only thing you can do because you’re at the mercy of medicine.”

Now in her senior year at USC, Isabella is looking ahead to life after graduation.

“[There’s] a lot of interesting opportunities and things that I want to pursue,” she said.

Michael has no doubt she will find her way.

“She’s so talented, and this experience, in my opinion, has opened up my eyes to more talent that she has that I didn’t realize…the talent to connect people, and be in front of a crowd. I always thought she’d be nervous because I get nervous, but she’s better than me,” he said.

#4865. Rivian’s electric van gets 30% more range and AWD, now delivering

Rivian has started delivering the first major hardware upgrade to its electric van since production began in 2021: a bigger LFP battery pack good for 30% more range, and a new dual-motor AWD version.

The company confirmed in its Q3 2026 shareholder presentation that deliveries of the new variants began in early October. That’s the first real spec bump for a van that has been stuck at about 160 miles of rated range for years.

Rivian first mentioned the upgrade in its Q4 2025 letter, which we covered in February when Amazon’s fleet of Rivian vans grew 50%. At the time, Rivian only said it was “developing” a larger battery and AWD to “expand EDV route coverage” in Amazon’s network.

Now it’s shipping. In today’s presentation, Rivian says the new variants are “specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks,” with the AWD configuration and the bigger pack offering “a 30% increase in range.”

EPA certification documents for the 2027 EDV 700, issued September 17, list the new pack at 129 kWh usable. Rivian has marketed the current van with a 100 kWh LFP pack, so that’s roughly 29% more energy, which lines up with the 30% range claim.

The upgrade is limited to the bigger 700 van, the one with 652 cubic feet of cargo space. The smaller 500 keeps its existing pack and front-wheel drive.

The EPA filing gives unadjusted lab range figures, which always run high because they skip the correction for real-world driving:

Rivian rates the current 700 at “up to 160 miles.” Apply Rivian’s 30% to that and the new FWD van lands around 208 miles. Using the AWD van’s smaller 23% gain from the EPA tests, we estimate the dual-motor version at about 195 to 200 miles.

So AWD costs roughly a third of the range gain. For a van, that’s a fine trade. Rural routes mean longer distances between stops, plus gravel, mud, and snow, which is exactly where a front-wheel-drive van with a full load of packages in the back struggles.

200 miles is roughly what Rivian promised for the van when deliveries to Amazon started in 2022, before the rated figure settled closer to 160 miles. Rivian is finally there, four years later.

The timing helps on the sales side too. Rivian’s van business is still overwhelmingly Amazon, years after the exclusivity period ended in late 2023. We spotted a Rivian van in Walmart+ livery on a car hauler in Indiana just this week, though neither company has announced a deal.

The competition has also thinned out. GM ended BrightDrop van production in Ontario and Canoo went bankrupt, leaving Ford’s E-Transit as the main full-size electric alternative in the US.

Rivian needs to make the sales to USPS. I am starting to see those vans all the time now. It looks like it is designed from ground up to optimize for delivery. Extra height for drivers, lower floor of entry, great visibility in the front. Low bumper and lower headlight position for safety. Overall, great design.

Too bad that GM dropped Brightdrop van just as they are getting popular. I see a lot of FedEx trucks are now Bright drop. Perfect timing when diesel price is thru the roof. GM never have the long term view and always good at starting something but give up just before it becomes a hot seller.

This is the upgrade the van needed. 160 miles was always fine for dense urban Amazon routes, but it boxed Rivian out of a big chunk of the fleet market: rural delivery, utilities, telecom, anyone who can’t guarantee a short loop and an overnight charge.

Getting to around 200 miles real-world, with AWD as an option, opens a lot of those routes. And unlike most of the EV van market right now, Rivian is actually building and improving its product rather than killing it.

The question is whether Rivian can turn that into customers other than Amazon. A Walmart+ wrap on a car hauler is a nice sign. We’d want to see a real order. If you’re running a fleet and these specs change your math, we’d love to hear from you.

Sitting in a sauna is a nice way to unwind, whether you're starting your day or coming down post-workout. But while it can feel good to lounge in the heat to decompress, research suggests you might be doing your immune system a solid in the process, too.

The study, which was published in the journal Temperature, found that hanging (or ‘bathing,’ as it’s called) in the sauna for 30 minutes sparks a unique chain reaction in the body that could support your health. Scientists haven't quite figured out what these changes mean when it comes to measurable impact on immunity, but doctors say this is definitely one more thing to mull over while you're getting your sauna on. Here's why.

Meet the experts: Jari Laukkanen, MD, PhD, study co-author and professor at the University of Eastern Finland; Eric Ascher, DO, family medicine physician at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital; and Joseph J. Ciotola, MD, an orthopedic surgeon at Baltimore's Mercy Medical Center

For the study, researchers recruited 51 adults with an average age of 50. Scientists took blood samples before asking participants to sit in a 163-degree sauna for 30 minutes. The participants gave blood samples again right after the sauna session and again 30 minutes later.

The researchers found that there was a temporary increase in every type of circulating white blood cell they measured, including immune cells called neutrophils and lymphocytes. Neutrophils are usually the first defenders to respond to an infection and lymphocytes recognize specific threats, make antibodies, and help coordinate immune responses. The increase only lasted for 30 minutes—the neutrophil and lymphocyte counts returned to baseline after that.

"We have studied sauna bathing and cardiovascular health for many years, and our previous studies have shown interesting associations with better health outcomes," says Jari Laukkanen, MD, PhD, study co-author and professor at the University of Eastern Finland. "We wanted to understand more about the biological mechanisms behind these findings, including possible effects on the immune system."

Again, the researchers simply found that this jump in certain white blood cells happens when someone sits in a sauna—they didn't figure out why it happens or what it means. Still, experts have a few theories.

One is that sauna bathing presents a sudden physical challenge for the body, according to Eric Ascher, DO, a family medicine physician at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital. "This heat stress wakes up your nervous system, causing white blood cells stored in different parts of your body to rush into your bloodstream," he says.

This is similar to what happens in the body when you do a cold plunge, says Joseph J. Ciotola, MD, an orthopedic surgeon at Baltimore's Mercy Medical Center. “It’s just hormetic stress,” he adds, referring to the process where short stressors can trigger a positive adaptive response in the body and make you stronger.

The release of these immune cells is also similar to what happens during physical exercise, Laukkanen says.

As for what this means for the body, that's still being explored. "White blood cells are important for immune defense and surveillance," Laukkanen says. "Their temporary mobilization may help the body respond to physiological challenges."

But Laukkanen also says that it's not clear yet what this means for immune health. "Our study measured acute responses after one sauna session, and we cannot yet say whether these changes improve long-term immunity or reduce the risk of infections," he says. "More research is needed."

You do more than just sweat in a sauna. "Saunas make your heart beat faster, and your blood vessels open up, which is very similar to the benefits you get from taking a brisk walk or going for a light run," Ascher says. "Because of this, regular sauna use has been linked to lower blood pressure, a healthier heart, and a lower risk of getting certain long-term diseases." (Still, he stresses that there's no data now to suggest that sauna use will replace the need for medication or exercise.)

Sauna use can also help people relax, recover from stress, and support overall well-being, Laukkanen says. "Sauna can be a pleasant part of a healthy lifestyle, alongside regular physical activity," he adds.

Of course, not everyone should hop in the sauna. "Because the intense heat puts a lot of stress on your heart and body, anyone with serious heart problems, very low blood pressure, or severe dizziness should stay out of saunas," Ascher says. Pregnant women and older adults may also want to steer clear.

But if you already like hanging in the sauna, it's nice to know you might be doing your immune system a solid while you kick back and enjoy.

#4862. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.

#4860. I Have a New Hobby. It’s Kicking My Ass.

The fastest-growing racquet sport in America may also be the cardio workout I’ve been avoiding.

This column first appeared in the Men’s Health email newsletter. The Optimized Man is a biweekly series from our editorial director as he tries out the latest, greatest, and weirdest health and wellness innovations so you don’t have to. Sign up here to get the next one.

I’VE TRIED TO build a life free of shoulds. I’m fine with woulds and coulds and their vague promise of actionability, but when you get into shoulds, you get hung up on stuff like guilt and doubt and all kinds of second-guessing. I really should work out. I really shouldn’t eat that. You think I should try and sleep more? Thanks, man. Good tip.

Shoulds, put plainly, are a problem, and this year I’ve been staring down two different shoulds that won’t quit staring back: I should probably do more cardio, and I should probably get a hobby. I’ve never been much of a cardio guy or a hobby guy, but with evidence tying both to better physical and mental health outcomes, my list of excuses for not doing either is growing short. And I think I’ve found a solution in one of the fastest-growing sports in America.

It’s called padel (pronounced pa-DEL), and you might’ve come across it if you’ve been on vacation lately in Central America or southern Europe (or somewhere really exotic, like Miami). I discovered it last year on a cold winter’s night, and after playing for two hours on an indoor court and emerging sweaty, sore, and exuberant, I can report that it combines everything I like about tennis, racquetball, and squash into one hard-hitting, heavy-breathing sport.

You can go ahead and YouTube the basics, and here’s the gist: You’re playing on a court that’s about three-quarters the area of a tennis court, with high glass walls along the back, some wire fencing on the sides, and a net down the middle. Instead of pickleball’s slow and endless dinking, a padel ball whirs fast off your midsize racquet (also larger and heavier than pickleball’s), and the action requires you to move. Even though it’s a doubles sport (which typically requires less movement than singles, ‘cause there’s two of you), you’re constantly chasing the ball like it’s that little golden bug in quidditch. Sprint, stop, swing, pivot, repeat. (You can also hit the ball against the back wall to launch it in reverse, back over the net, which requires a massive swing.) The first time I played, I showed up wearing sweatpants and a puffer vest over a T-shirt. Within minutes of starting I had sweat through my T-shirt, and by the end of the first set, I had sweat through the seat of my sweatpants. I looked like John Candy in Splash, post-racquetball. What can I say? I’m not a cardio guy.

And there is a lot of cardio here. Back in 2024 we noticed that tennis had started billing itself as “the world’s healthiest sport,” and we asked writer Nick Pachelli to dig into the branding to see how much of it is hype. According to Nick:

Padel isn’t tennis and tennis isn’t padel, but I’ve been playing tennis for almost four decades, and I’ve never had my ass kicked quite as hard as when I played padel.

Then there is the social aspect of it—you’re part of a pair playing another pair, and whether you’re close friends or total strangers with your partner or opponents, at least you’re not bowling alone. Nick found that when longevity researchers study tennis…

Aerobic exercise, social connection and community, some light competition, and a lot of laughs: Could padel be my new hobby? Could it be my main source of cardio? Winter’s coming and the indoor courts are calling, and with visions of John Candy huffing and puffing in my head, I should probably start training.

Richard Dorment is the editorial director of Men’s Health and Women’s Health.

#4858. Heart Failure Is Becoming More Common in Adults Under 65, Report Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023, more than double the number in 1990, according to a new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analysis published September 30 in JAMA Cardiology.

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Despite its name, heart failure doesn’t mean the heart has stopped beating.

A separate 2026 report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) found that heart failure contributed to more than 450,000 deaths in the United States in 2023, with particularly sharp increases in mortality among adults under 65.

Approximately 7.7 million U.S. adults (3%) are living with heart failure, according to the HFSA report. That number is projected to rise to 8.7 million by 2030, 10.3 million by 2040, and 11.4 million by 2050.

The GBD researchers said the findings highlight the growing burden of heart failure associated with population growth and aging, as well as the need for prevention and treatment strategies targeting common causes such as ischemic heart disease and hypertension (high blood pressure).

Between 2010 and 2022, heart failure hospitalization rates increased among adults under 65 while declining among those 65 and older. Between 2001 and 2020, estimated heart failure mortality rates more than doubled among adults ages 25 to 44 and nearly doubled among those ages 45 to 64.

“I think we’re seeing the impact of cardiovascular risk factors developing earlier in life. Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea are affecting younger adults at higher rates than in previous generations,” Kevin Shah, MD, Program Director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the analysis, told Healthline.

“When those risk factors are present for decades, they can eventually lead to heart failure at a younger age,” he said.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist at Manhattan Cardiology in New York City who was also not involved in the analysis, noted that improvements in early detection may also play a role.

“Our tools to detect early heart failure are also improving with time, and as a result, patients may receive an earlier diagnosis and can hopefully start medical therapy to prevent progression or possibly even reverse the process entirely.”

Heart failure contributed to 452,573 deaths in the United States in 2023, accounting for approximately 14.6% of all deaths that year, according to the HFSA report.

Age-adjusted heart failure mortality rates increased by approximately 37% between 2010 and 2023, with preliminary 2024 data suggesting the upward trend is continuing.

This increase appears to have reversed more than a decade of previous progress in reducing heart failure mortality.

Ischemic heart disease and hypertension were among the most common causes of heart failure in older adults, according to the GBD report. However, the underlying causes varied considerably by age group and region.

Among children and young adults, congenital heart abnormalities and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common causes of heart failure. Heart failure associated with alcohol use was most prevalent during middle adulthood.

The analysis also identified regional differences in the underlying causes of heart failure:

The global burden of heart failure is expected to grow as populations age.

While not all cases of heart failure can be prevented, managing certain risk factors can help reduce your risk. These include:

According to Shah, other important steps to help prevent heart failure include maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, and managing conditions such as diabetes and high cholesterol.

He added that regular medical care is important because many of these risk factors can be identified and treated long before heart failure develops.

“Heart failure is often treatable and may even be reversible with early diagnosis and treatment. It is important for patients to seek help early if they have concerning symptoms, such as exertional shortness of breath, chest pain, leg swelling, or anything else they’re concerned about. Talk with your doctors early and often,” said Blumfield.

#4857. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

#4856. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

#4855. How to Know You're Going Through 'Couple Burnout'

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

A research paper published in Social Psychology Quarterly introduces a 10-item scale that measures “burnout” within couples, providing mental health experts and the public with a tool that can help couples address feelings of exhaustion and indifference within their relationships.

According to the researchers, burnout refers to feelings of mental, physical, and emotional exhaustion that lead to feelings of disengagement and a lowered sense of accomplishment. It is often the result of over-involvement in emotionally demanding responsibilities.

Although burnout is commonly understood as a work-related experience, studies show that burnout can occur within romantic relationships, too. The exhaustion we’re used to feeling after a long and stressful day of work can also be felt when we disconnect or detach from our partner. Even more concerning, these two types of burnout can interact with one another in detrimental ways.

In the study, the authors explain that the experience of burnout in one area of life can spill over into others. In essence, if you’re experiencing stress or strain in your relationship, there is a decent chance that you’ll experience burnout in your work life, too.

Moreover, the researchers also found that one partner’s experience of burnout can cross over to the other partner. Essentially, if one partner expresses stress with their work or in the relationship, the other partner’s experience of burnout may also increase.

These findings highlight how burnout isn’t just a one-dimensional issue; it’s a contagion that can spread between different aspects of one’s life. If you’re feeling overwhelmed or strained in your relationship, it’s likely to spill into your work life, and vice versa.

When we’re burning the candle at both ends, our well-being suffers. And perhaps the most eye-opening discovery is that burnout isn’t just an individual struggle—it’s a shared experience in couples.

To measure the experience of burnout in couples, the researchers developed a 10-item scale that captures symptoms of emotional, mental, and physical exhaustion in a romantic partnership.

The test, intended to be answered on a scale from “never” to “always,” is as follows:

When you think about your marriage or intimate relationship overall, how often have you felt:

If you frequently grapple with these 10 feelings, you might be experiencing couple’s burnout. The best thing you can do in this situation is to reach out to your partner and let them in on your feelings and experiences.

Remember, you’re not alone. Burnout often infiltrates the relationship space like an uninvited guest. By actively supporting one another, communicating openly, and making a conscious effort to re-center yourselves, you’re not just tackling burnout as individuals; you’re navigating it as a team.

The significance of supporting each other when one or both partners are experiencing burnout cannot be overstated. It’s like holding an umbrella together in a rainstorm—you shield each other from the downpour. Finding that balance, both in the hustle of your careers and the intimacy of your romantic life, isn’t just an option, but a lifeline. It’s the key to surviving and thriving in your relationship.

#4854. How This Busy Dad Got Leaner and Stronger in 11 Weeks Without Losing Much Weight

Strength coach Gareth Sapstead shares how he helped a busy dad and business owner get leaner, build muscle, and reshape his physique.

Body recomposition is widely viewed as the holy grail of physical transformation: losing body fat while simultaneously adding lean muscle.

It’s also often dismissed as either impossible or reserved exclusively for complete beginners. The logic appears fairly convincing. To lose fat, you need to consume fewer calories than you burn. To build muscle, you need enough energy to construct new tissue. One requires a deficit, the other seemingly demands a surplus.

Pick a lane: bulk first, cut later. Right?

Strength and physique coach Gareth Sapstead disagrees. In a detailed breakdown published on his website, Sapstead explains how he helped father and business owner Mark Schadenberg transform his physique ahead of a Men’s Health Netherlands photoshoot—losing fat, adding visible muscle and finishing just 4 pounds lighter after 11 weeks.

The scales barely budged, but his body changed dramatically.

“The fitness industry has been telling you to pick one for decades,” says Sapstead. “Bulk first, cut later. Build the muscle, then reveal it.”

Sapstead accepts that fat loss requires an energy deficit, while building muscle requires energy. However, he says the apparent contradiction comes from treating your body like a single energy account.

“Fat tissue and muscle tissue operate through different pathways,” he explains. “You can be breaking down stored fat for fuel while simultaneously building muscle protein—as long as the conditions for muscle protein synthesis are met.”

Those conditions are relatively straightforward: enough protein and a sufficiently challenging resistance-training stimulus.

Sapstead points towards research examining simultaneous fat loss and muscle gain. According to Sapstead, the phenomenon appeared consistently across the research and wasn’t simply a beginner-only fluke.

He also references studies in which participants consumed between 400 and 800 additional calories each day, all from protein.

By conventional logic, those extra calories should have resulted in weight gain. Instead, Sapstead says the participants either maintained their weight or lost fat while gaining or preserving muscle.

“Body recomposition is real,” he concludes. “It’s well-supported, and for the right person in the right circumstances, it happens faster than most expect.”

Schadenberg had just 11 weeks to prepare for his photoshoot. He was running a business and raising a family—a familiar combination for many of us—that had gradually pushed training, nutrition, and recovery down his list of priorities.

“He’d let his training slip,” says Sapstead. “Not from a lack of drive, but through the entirely predictable reality of running a business and raising a family.”

His sleep was suffering, his diet lacked structure and he had no consistent exercise routine. Like many men in their late 30s and 40s, Sapstead says, he was also “chronically undereating protein.”

That might not sound like an ideal starting point, but it gave Schadenberg several powerful variables to improve almost immediately.

“Every one of those factors is a recomposition accelerant,” says Sapstead.

Returning to resistance training after a significant lay-off can produce a response closer to that of a beginner. The stimulus feels novel again, adaptations arrive quickly and previously built muscle may return faster than it took to develop in the first place.

Combine that with more protein, better recovery and structured training, and you can create the conditions to rebuild muscle while using stored body fat to help cover the energy costs.

“The body has been starved of the right inputs,” says Sapstead. “Give it protein, training and adequate recovery, and it responds.”

After 11 weeks, Schadenberg was only 4 pounds lighter. But his before-and-after photographs showed considerably more muscle and significantly less body fat.

“Fat came off. Muscle went on. Bodyweight barely moved,” says Sapstead.

Sapstead says recomposition is particularly well suited to anyone who has been away from consistent strength training, is carrying more body fat than they would like, habitually eats too little protein or has allowed sleep and recovery to deteriorate.

For experienced lifters who have trained intelligently, eaten well, and slept properly for years, the process is likely to be slower. There’s simply less low-hanging fruit.

For returning lifters, however, they're in a prime position for a recomp.

This isn’t the time for an aggressive diet or an uncontrolled bulk. Sapstead recommends eating around your maintenance calories or slightly above them, with approximately 200 to 300 additional calories coming predominantly from protein.

The aim is to provide enough energy to support training and muscle growth without creating a large surplus that encourages unnecessary fat gain.

Sapstead sets protein at around one gram per pound of bodyweight as a starting point, although higher intakes may also be appropriate.

Protein provides the raw materials required to repair and construct muscle tissue. It is also highly satiating, making it easier to control your overall food intake without constantly feeling hungry.

Perform three to four structured resistance-training sessions each week, with a focus on progressive overload.

Your body needs a reason to preserve and build muscle. That means gradually adding weight, completing more reps, improving your range of motion or producing better-quality work—not simply getting hot and tired doing random circuits, or going through the motions with zero intensity.

When fat is coming off while muscle is being added, your bodyweight may barely change. That doesn’t mean the approach has stopped working. It may mean it’s working exactly as intended.

“The scale would have told him nothing was happening,” Sapstead says of Schadenberg’s transformation. “The photos would have told him everything.”

Take progress pictures every two to three weeks, track your gym performance and pay attention to how your clothes fit. If your waist is shrinking, your strength is improving and you look more muscular, a stable bodyweight isn’t failure—it’s the holy grail of body recomp in action.

With almost 18 years in the health and fitness space as a personal trainer, nutritionist, breath coach and writer, Andrew has spent nearly half of his life exploring how to help people improve their bodies and minds.

As our fitness editor he prides himself on keeping Men’s Health at the forefront of reliable, relatable and credible fitness information, whether that’s through writing and testing thousands of workouts each year, taking deep dives into the science behind muscle building and fat loss or exploring the psychology of performance and recovery.

Whilst constantly updating his knowledge base with seminars and courses, Andrew is a lover of the practical as much as the theory and regularly puts his training to the test tackling everything from Crossfit and strongman competitions, to ultra marathons, to multiple 24 hour workout stints and (extremely unofficial) world record attempts.

#4853. PMOS, Formerly PCOS, May Be Associated with Alzheimer's Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), has been linked to changes in brain function and cognition that may overlap with those seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

However, a review published October 13 in the Journal of the Endocrine Society suggests that metabolic conditions commonly associated with PMOS, rather than PMOS itself, may help explain a potential link to Alzheimer’s disease and dementia risk.

“Researchers are exploring whether some metabolic conditions commonly seen in women with PMOS, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, [and] elevated cholesterol, could play a role in dementia, since these are already known risk factors for cognitive decline,” Yesika Garcia, MD, board certified endocrinologist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline.

“In other words, any potential connection may be related to these underlying metabolic issues rather than PMOS itself. I think it’s important to clarify that an association does not mean causation,” she added.

The researchers searched PubMed for studies published through 2025 examining brain structure and function, cognitive performance, biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and dementia risk in people with PMOS.

Because PMOS is a newer term, the researchers searched for studies using both PMOS and PCOS.

The review identified studies suggesting that people with PMOS may experience mild differences in certain cognitive abilities, including:

Some brain imaging studies using MRI and PET scans identified differences in brain structure and function among people with PMOS. Researchers also observed hormonal changes associated with differences in gray matter.

Some studies identified elevated biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease in people with PMOS. These findings appeared to overlap with metabolic changes seen in type 2 diabetes, particularly those associated with obesity and insulin resistance.

The researchers also found that neurological differences were less pronounced when people with PMOS were compared with metabolically healthy control groups, suggesting that associated metabolic conditions may play an important role in these findings.

Overall, the review suggests that metabolic conditions associated with PMOS may contribute to changes in brain health, although more research is needed to determine whether PMOS independently affects Alzheimer’s disease or dementia risk.

“I think we need to be careful about drawing conclusions too early. The research raises some good questions, but it doesn’t prove that PCOS [PMOS] causes Alzheimer’s disease,” said Dung Trinh, MD, internist, of MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“What it does reinforce is how important metabolic health may be when it comes to protecting our brains as we get older,” he added.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed. She also added that more attention and research need to be given to PMOS, brain changes, and future risks of dementia.

There are various ways that PMOS and dementia may share pathways and overlap, according to the researchers. Some of these shared pathways include:

Trinh explained that insulin resistance may be one of the most important connections between PMOS and dementia.

Although insulin is commonly associated with diabetes and blood sugar regulation, it also plays an important role in brain function. When insulin signaling doesn’t work properly, it may interfere with how brain cells use energy, potentially contributing to problems with memory and thinking over time.

Chronic inflammation, which can occur in people with PMOS, may also play a role in Alzheimer’s disease, Trinh told Healthline.

“Researchers are looking at how these metabolic changes may affect amyloid and tau, two proteins associated with Alzheimer’s. Some brain imaging studies have even found differences in brain structure and function among women with PCOS [PMOS],” he said.

Ross added that elevated androgen levels, which are common in people with PMOS, may also play a role in dementia risk.

“An important distinction is that these risk factors are not present in every woman with PMOS, and having PMOS does not automatically mean someone will experience cognitive decline,” cautioned Garcia.

Garcia noted that many of the dementia risk factors associated with PMOS are modifiable.

“Regular exercise, including both cardiovascular activity and strength training, can improve insulin sensitivity, help with weight management, and support cardiovascular and brain health,” she added.

“A Mediterranean-style diet, with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean sources of protein, is a reasonable place to start,” he said.

Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure is also important, Trinh and Garcia noted.

“Medication, like metformin, can also improve insulin resistance, which may further reduce the risk of dementia,” Ross added.

Getting adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and staying mentally and socially active are additional ways to support long-term brain health, Garcia told Healthline.

“For someone with PCOS [PMOS], I would encourage regular visits with their healthcare provider to monitor metabolic health and address problems early,” said Trinh.

“While we cannot say that these interventions specifically prevent dementia in women with PMOS, we know they benefit overall metabolic and cardiovascular health, which are closely connected to brain health,” explained Garcia.

#4852. When Someone You Love Suddenly Feels Like the Enemy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Imagine you're telling your partner about a frustrating phone call you had with your mom, and they jokingly remark, "Well, we all know how much you love being right."

You know they're teasing, but you feel yourself starting to get angry. In fact, without meaning to, you’re now thinking of the last time your partner made an off-color comment. And the time before that. Before you know it, you’ve written them off as insensitive and uncaring. Despite starting the evening looking forward to hanging out together, you’re now questioning whether you even want to be with this person.

Yes, your partner's comment was insensitive, and it's certainly reasonable to feel hurt. At the same time, in the heat of the moment, that single interaction has overshadowed all the positive experiences you've shared and the qualities you usually appreciate about your partner.

For people with borderline personality disorder (BPD), experiences like this are really common. In fact, alternating between idealizing and devaluing others is one of the diagnostic criteria for this condition. When things are going smoothly, a partner, friend, or family member might seem like the most loving, supportive person in the world. However, that same person may suddenly seem selfish or untrustworthy after a disappointing interaction.

This pattern is sometimes called splitting, a form of black-and-white thinking in which people have difficulty holding positive and negative qualities in mind at the same time. Rather than recognizing that someone can be a caring partner who occasionally says something insensitive, the negative experience overshadows everything else.

These sudden shifts in how we perceive the people closest to us can be disorienting, making it difficult to maintain stable, lasting relationships. Indeed, negative perceptions of others, however temporary, can lead to behaviors that cause lasting consequences. For example, if you're convinced your partner doesn't care about you, you might lash out, accuse them of being selfish, or threaten to end the relationship. Alternatively, you might withdraw, stop responding to messages, or push them away before they have the chance to reject you.

In BPD Compass, an evidence-based treatment for BPD, there are two strategies that are particularly relevant for combating the difficulties all-or-nothing thinking can cause.

The first is the Relationship Compass, a tool for deciding your goals for a given relationship. The Relationship Compass replaces the cardinal directions (North, South, East, and West) with relationship objectives: I Need something; I want to Set a limit; I Want to get closer; I’m considering Ending a relationship.

The Relationship Compass helps you identify what you ultimately want from a relationship before you're in the middle of an upsetting interaction. That way, when your emotions threaten to take the wheel, you’ll have already planned behaviors that align with your compass.

Another important strategy from BPD Compass is the Dimensions of Trust exercise. Here, you’re asked to consider the various ways you can trust the specific people in your life. The dimensions on which other people are rated (0 to 100 percent) include the degree to which someone is on time, emotionally supportive, does what they say they’re going to do, keeps your confidences, is trusted to watch your kids, etc.

Not only do you get to see that most people fall somewhere between 0 and 100 percent on any given dimension, but you also begin to recognize that someone can be highly trustworthy in some areas and less so in others. The next time you're tempted to write someone off as completely untrustworthy, you can revisit these ratings to remind yourself of the bigger picture and decide how to respond based on their actual strengths and limitations.

Together, these strategies create some distance between how we feel about someone in a particular moment and how we choose to respond. We can acknowledge that someone has hurt us without losing sight of everything else we know about them or the relationship.

No matter how solid a relationship may be, there will be times when you hurt each other's feelings. It is important to recognize those shortcomings without allowing them to erase everything else we know about that person.

For people with BPD, this can take practice. Over time, you can get better at seeing your relationships in shades of gray; in other words, it is possible to see both the positive and negative qualities of someone at the same time. As you strengthen this ability, you’ll also get better at choosing reactions that align with what you ultimately want, rather than how you feel in a particular moment.

Want to build healthier, more stable relationships? The BPD Compass Companion Course teaches practical, evidence-based skills for managing intense emotions and navigating relationship difficulties.

#4851. RJ Mitte's Death Highlights Mental Health Challenges for People With Cerebral Palsy

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Breaking Bad” actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte has died at age 34.

Mitte reportedly died by suicide, his representative told People on October 12. However, local authorities have said the official cause and manner of his death remain under investigation.

Mitte, who was best-known for playing Walter White Jr. on the Emmy Award-winning television series “Breaking Bad,” lived with cerebral palsy and advocated for disability inclusion.

There is currently no evidence to suggest that cerebral palsy caused the actor’s death. Still, Mitte’s untimely passing highlights the mental health challenges that people with cerebral palsy may face.

Research has demonstrated elevated risks of anxiety and depression among those with the condition, alongside barriers to diagnosis, social participation, and employment.

“Living with cerebral palsy can affect mental health through several interacting pathways,” said Shannel Elhelou, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, CA.

“Chronic pain, fatigue, disrupted sleep, and the effort required to navigate daily activities can take an emotional toll. Experiences of bullying, discrimination, social exclusion, and difficulty accessing care can add to that burden. Also, the early brain injury underlying cerebral palsy may contribute to difficulties with emotional regulation, although each person’s experience is different,” Elhelou told Healthline.

If you or someone you know is in crisis and considering suicide or self-harm, please seek support:

If you’re calling on behalf of someone else, stay with them until help arrives. You may remove weapons or substances that can cause harm if you can do so safely.

If you’re not in the same household, stay on the phone with them until help arrives.

Mitte played a key role in challenging stereotypes by portraying a teenager with cerebral palsy on “Breaking Bad.”

Outside of acting, Mitte advocated for people with disabilities through organizations including United Cerebral Palsy (UCP) and Shriners Children’s.

He also led the Mitte Foundation, a non-profit corporation founded in 1994 by his grandparents, Roy F. and Joann Cole Mitte, that improves the quality of life for people in Central Texas.

Mitte’s advocacy emphasized representation, inclusion, and opportunities for people with disabilities.

The legacy he leaves behind underscores the need to recognize mental health as an essential part of care for individuals with cerebral palsy and other disabilities.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of conditions affecting movement, posture, and coordination.

Most people with cerebral palsy have typical intelligence, although some also have intellectual disabilities or other comorbid physical and mental health conditions.

A 2018 study published in JAMA Neurology found that adults with cerebral palsy had a 28% higher risk of developing depression and a 40% higher risk of anxiety than adults without the condition.

A 2024 study in JAMA Network Open found higher recorded rates of anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) among children and young adults with cerebral palsy.

The researchers also identified comparatively low rates of depression and suicidal ideation, highlighting concerns that these conditions may be underdiagnosed.

“Research shows that adults with cerebral palsy have an increased risk of depression and anxiety,” Elhelou said.

“However, these conditions should never be viewed as an inevitable part of having a disability. One concern is ‘diagnostic overshadowing,’ when symptoms of depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions are attributed to cerebral palsy itself, leading those conditions to go unrecognized and untreated. Someone’s fatigue, withdrawal, or changes in behavior deserve careful assessment rather than the assumption that ‘this is just their cerebral palsy,'” she continued.

“While these findings help us understand mental health risks among people with cerebral palsy, they cannot tell us what any one person was experiencing. Many interacting factors may contribute to someone dying by suicide, and it would be inappropriate to attribute an individual’s death to their disability.”

A 2019 study published in Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology found that children with cerebral palsy had higher odds of anxiety disorders and behavioral challenges than children without the condition.

Difficulties with friendships and bullying were associated with some of these differences.

Factors that may affect well-being include:

The researchers also found that supportive friendships may help reduce some of these disparities, reinforcing the importance of inclusive schools and communities.

A 2021 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that U.S. adults with disabilities faced increased risks of suicidal thoughts, planning, and attempts compared with adults without disabilities.

The 988 Lifeline received more than 8 million contacts through calls, texts, chats, and American Sign Language videophone in 2025, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Federal funding for the Lifeline’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth service ended in July 2025, removing the option to press 3 for specialized support.

After pressure from Congress, the service was recently restored at the end of September, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF).

Employment and financial independence can influence well-being for anyone, particularly those with cerebral palsy.

However, a 2024 study found that just 30.4% of young adults with cerebral palsy who participated in vocational rehabilitation programs were employed when they exited those programs.

Workplace accommodations, accessible hiring, vocational rehabilitation, and inclusive social opportunities can help address these barriers.

“Depression and anxiety are treatable, and they should never be dismissed as an inevitable part of living with a disability,” Elhelou said.

“If you notice persistent sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or withdrawal, reach out to someone you trust and a mental health professional. You deserve a clinician who takes your concerns seriously and adapts treatment to your communication, mobility, or other access needs. Care should also address pain, fatigue, and sleep difficulties, which can affect emotional well-being.”

Organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy offer information and support for people with cerebral palsy and their families.

Healthcare professionals can also improve outcomes by screening for mental health concerns, using appropriate assessment tools, and connecting patients with accessible treatment.

Improved access to care, inclusive communities, and meaningful opportunities can help people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities thrive.

“Asking for help does not diminish your resilience or your contributions. If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide or feel overwhelmed, you do not have to wait until things feel unbearable to reach out,” Elhelou said.

“Supportive relationships, peer groups, and disability communities can offer connection and understanding. Staying engaged in activities that bring enjoyment and meaning can also help.”
