#4850. Why Cognitive Surrender Feels Alright

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Imagine your boss asks you to analyze some data and then write up a report on it. You are already busy with several projects and approaching deadlines for other reports, so you generate a draft of the report using an AI tool. The report looks polished, tells a coherent and sensible story about the data, and includes statistics to back up its points.

Do you check for typos, then turn it in? Or do you read it carefully and check it against your own analysis of the data?

The first choice would be considered “cognitive surrender.”

Cognitive surrender means handing over critical thinking or judgment to an AI tool instead of doing it yourself. It is moving from using AI to augment your thinking to using it to do your thinking.

This can lead to serious problems, including becoming worse at critical thinking. When you offload critical thinking to technology, your ability to do that kind of thinking can erode, because the skills of thinking aren’t practiced. Of course, another problem with cognitive surrender is that AI can be wrong. When you do it on something important (e.g., a class grade, a major project at work, a big financial decision), there could be terrible consequences.

Considering those possible consequences of cognitive surrender, why would anyone do it? There are several psychological phenomena that might make it quite easy to surrender even if you don’t intend to. Here are three:

These research findings, however, could also point us towards strategies for using AI more safely and effectively.

First, don’t seize on the first answer AI gives you. Interrogate the tool, ask it to argue another perspective, or ask it to give sources that support its conclusions, and go and read them. One important thing to remember is that most AIs are trained to deliver what users most like, not necessarily what’s most accurate. So, resist the temptation to accept the first answer.

Second, think of an AI answer as a sales pitch. During development, AI models are generally rewarded for being confident. Just like you might discount a salesperson’s confidence about their product, you may want to discount an AI’s confidence in its conclusions and answers.

And third, if you want your critical thinking skills to stay sharp, you probably need to practice them. If you find yourself outsourcing a lot of hard mental work to AI tools, you could hold back and go through the difficult slog on some of that work. Just like working hard physically makes your body healthier, working hard mentally may keep your brain healthier.

Some of these strategies can be done with a few extra prompts. Because AI tools are so good at following instructions, you can instruct them to help you avoid cognitive surrender if you want to.

Uncritically accepting AI output can be helpful at times, especially when you have crafted appropriate prompts, built a custom agent, or otherwise analyzed how the tool will handle its assignment. But the costs of this surrender could sometimes outweigh the convenience and productivity boost.

#4849. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

#4848. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

#4847. Why Your Wife Doesn’t Want Sex (and What Actually Helps)

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Arms crossed, jaw tight, eyes on the floor. As a couples therapist, I see this man in my office all the time. He says, “I’m tired of being the only one who wants it.” When you’ve been turned down over and over, it starts to feel less like what you’re hearing is “not tonight,” and more like it’s “not you.”

Maybe you feel like you have tried everything to make your partner want sex with you. It just seems like she never does, no matter what you do. Beyond feeling sexually frustrated, you feel rejected, unwanted, and unattractive. You may tell yourself stories that something is wrong with you, like your sexual performance or the way you look, or stories about how your wife is the problem, such as that she has a “low libido” and needs to work on her desire herself.

These stories make sense. They’re also usually wrong.

Desire discrepancies are common. Far from being the exception, differences in sexual desire are a part of most relationships (Fogel Mersy & Vencill, 2023). Your relationship is probably normal. And so is your wife.

Your wife not wanting sex out of the blue is not the same as your wife not wanting sex with you. She probably does experience sexual desire, just not in the way that you expect.

Most men (75%) have a primarily “spontaneous” desire style; the feeling of randomly, out of the blue, wanting sex. However, for most women, sexual arousal actually precedes the feeling of sexual desire. Only 15% of women experience primarily spontaneous desire; the other 85% of women experience “responsive desire,” meaning sexual desire that occurs in response to sexual arousal or sexual stimuli. Let me say that again: for women, most often, physiological arousal comes first, and sexual desire comes after.

In my opinion, this is far and away the most common misconception about sex there is. Blame it on the patriarchy: because most of our ideas about sexuality are based on the “male as default,” most people in our society expect women’s sexual desire to be just like the average man’s. If spontaneous desire is the only kind you’ve ever experienced, it’s easy to assume it’s the only kind.

What you can do is create the conditions where her desire has room to show up. You can help her want sex by doing a few things: (1) help reduce her stress and fatigue, (2) build arousal for her pleasure, (3) cut the pressure.

Your wife, just like you, has two competing parts of her nervous system: the parasympathetic “rest-and-digest” branch and the sympathetic “fight-or-flight” branch. It’s hard for your wife to want to have sex when her body feels that a predator is chasing her. And more often than not, the stimuli that are activating her threat response are not actual predators. They are the mental load, unequal household and childcare work, body image, worry about whether her desire is “normal,” and feeling like sex is a debt she owes. It’s hard to feel sexy while mentally running the grocery list, the pediatrician appointment, and tomorrow’s carpool.

I see a self-reinforcing cycle in my couple clients. Stress reduces desire, and reduced desire creates more stress, which further reduces desire.

And your wife’s worry about letting you down becomes another thing that shuts down her desire.

You initiate, and she says, “Not tonight.” You feel rejected and either push harder or withdraw into sulking and resentment. Your wife feels pressure or guilt, her stress rises, and desire drops further. You feel more rejected. You’re doing what makes sense. It just doesn’t work.

You may have noticed that your wife starts to turn down not just sex, but non-sexual physical touch as well. When she associates every touch with pressure for sex, her body learns to brace against touch. And you end up feeling even more unwanted and far away.

The chasing dynamic (Nagoski, 2015) is the enemy, not your partner, not you.

Affection with no destination. To break out of the chasing cycle, touch needs to be uncoupled from pressure for sex. You need to touch, hug, kiss, and seek closeness with your wife without the expectation that it will lead to sex. Paradoxically, you’ll likely have more sex when you stop pushing for it. And make it ok for your wife to say no. No sulking, guilt-tripping, or expressing anger when she turns you down. The safer it is for her to say no, the easier it becomes for her to say yes.

Build arousal for her pleasure, not as a route to yes. The goal should be connection and mutual enjoyment. Sex is a possible outcome of touch, but it needs to be far from the target. Ask her what makes her feel cared for and loved, and do those things. Safety is the baseline for responsive desire. Get curious about what kinds of touch or words turn her on and activate her desire.

Lighten her load, but not as a trade. There’s a reason couples who share household chores more fairly have sex more often than couples where she carries most of the load (Carlson et al., 2016). And it’s not because she’s punishing you for leaving dishes in the sink or rewarding you for vacuuming. It’s because when she doesn’t have to carry stress alone, she moves out of fight-or-flight and into a nervous system state where her body is more likely to feel desire.

One important caveat here: if you clean the house so you’ll get sex, she will feel it, and it will just add more pressure. Show her that this is about her well-being, not yours.

When I explain responsive desire to husbands, their shoulders drop, and their jaws loosen. They start to understand that there is hope for a better sex life. There’s nothing wrong with you, your wife, or your marriage.

Work with your wife’s nervous system to help her responsive desire come online. Help lower her stress by taking things off her plate, like the laundry. Help her feel safe by removing the pressure. When safety is mixed with physiological arousal, desire has room to show up. The fastest way to her desire turns out to be the long way around.

#4845. Waymo picks Toyota bZ4X as its next robotaxi, starting in Japan in 2027

Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup. Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.

It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year. And it gives Waymo a Japanese-built car for its Tokyo launch, with the UK and other markets to follow.

When Waymo and Toyota first announced their deal in April 2025, it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles. Lots of intent, no product.

Now there’s a product. According to Waymo’s announcement, Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.

The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting. Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.

Operations in 2027 are about testing and validating the autonomous bZ4X fleet in Japan. The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.

The two companies also say they’ll keep working on autonomous tech for Toyota’s personal vehicles, plus safety projects with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software arm.

Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”

The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.

In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces. It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028.

The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.

For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900. A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.

And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it picked Toronto as its first Canadian city earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.

This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.

Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.

If Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning a personal vehicle, they are likely working on it. It doesn’t mean that it is going to happen but it’s obviously an avenue that they are both willing to explore. If things work out and they are actually able to bring a fully autonomous vehicle to market, that’s an extremely significant advantage from a top legacy car manufacturer that ultimately changes the game for Toyota and could potentially put them in the middle of the competition with other EV manufacturers.

Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off). But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable. And for a robotaxi, boring and reliable is the whole point.

Compare that with Tesla’s approach: a two-seat Cybercab with no steering wheel, built in-house, with a self-certified autonomy stack that still isn’t operating at anything close to Waymo’s scale. Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city. So far, that’s working.

The way it is looking now. It sounds like Toyota will take over manufacturing Waymo driver cars for right-hand-drive markets. But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle. Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete. If Toyota actually puts the Waymo Driver in a car you can buy, Tesla’s FSD Supervised pitch gets a lot harder to sell. Will that happen before the end of the decade? Who knows.

#4844. Pope Leo XIV Diagnosed With Lung Cancer After Surgery to Remove Part of Lung

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.

#4843. Volkswagen hits pause on the Golf EV as it faces an ‘urgent need for action’

Volkswagen has put the electric Golf on hold for now as it faces growing pressure to cut costs.

“We cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively,” Volkswagen Group CFO and COO Arno Antlitz warned after the company reported its largest quarterly loss since the “Dieselgate” scandal in 2015 on Thursday.

VW Group’s operating loss swelled to €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter because of a write-down of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and lower profit margins on electric vehicles.

As part of its latest cost-control efforts, Volkswagen is pausing development of the all-electric Golf at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said in an internal memo Reuters reviewed on Friday. The Wolfsburg plant, or the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Schäfer said the “decision was really not an easy one for us,” knowing what the Golf means to Wolfsburg.

The decision comes after Volkswagen’s Supervisory Board approved its restructuring strategy, “Future Plan 2030,” last month, which includes reducing its global workforce by 100,000, trimming its lineup, and closing several plants in Germany.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer confirmed earlier this year that the electric hatch will be delayed until closer to 2030.

It should be noted that they paid out dividends of 2.6 billion in August. Most of it went to 3 majority shareholders. But they used a clever accounting trick to delay the losses till now, just before talks with unions about pay.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected.

The electric Golf, which is expected to arrive as the ID. Golf, will be one of the first vehicles based on the new platform.

While development is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay the Golf EV’s launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030.

Volkswagen will begin building the electric Golf in Wolfsburg closer to the end of the decade, while production of the gas-powered model will move to Mexico in 2027.

#4842. Why Our Country Needs More School Psychologists

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Imagine it’s your first day of second grade. You’re feeling a mix of excitement and nervousness as you walk to your classroom. You walk into the wrong one and are greeted with stares from third graders. You quickly turn around and leave the room when you accidentally bump into someone. You look up, and a smiling face greets you, radiating immense warmth, and asks if you’re lost. You nod your head, and tears begin to well in your eyes. This person reassures you and asks you to take a deep “whale breath” before walking you to your classroom and then gives you a high five.

That person is a school psychologist, and our country needs more of them. In November, the National Association of School Psychologists (NASP) celebrates National School Psychology Week, which recognizes the essential roles they have within schools and communities. The role of school psychologists is so essential that NASP, the American Psychological Association (APA), and even former President Joe Biden have all called attention to the shortage of school psychologists in this country. Experts recommend that schools have one school psychologist for every 500 children, yet the national average is more than 1,000 students to one school psychologist. Despite all this, the profession of school psychology continues to be diminished by other branches of psychology, as well as misunderstood or unknown to lay people.

Think of a school psychologist as a special education teacher, administrator, counselor, and advocate all in one. School psychologists administer psychological assessments; facilitate individual and group counseling; perform interventions; participate in collaborations between schools, communities, and families; engage in consultation; advocate for systems-level changes; and more. School psychologists are known to “wear different hats” due to the broad range of skills that they employ on any given work day. Their strengths and talents know no bounds.

The official practice of school psychology emerged in 1896 when Lightner Witmer opened the first psychology clinic at the University of Pennsylvania. Witmer, considered the founder of both clinical and school psychology, created this clinic to develop remediation plans for children presenting with learning, attention, and behavioral problems in school. Many of the children assessed in his clinic met criteria for what is now understood as dyslexia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability. The children assessed in his clinic were referred to by teachers, parents, and other school-based professionals.

In his clinic, Witmer and his multidisciplinary team of physicians, social workers, and other professionals worked to diagnose children’s presenting problems through the “clinical method.” This method involved a referral system, testing, review of records, and treatment, which more closely resembled “modern school psychology than it would be to today’s practice of clinical psychology.” Witmer even discreetly implied that the “clinical psychologist” was in fact a “school psychologist,” thus prompting the graduate level of instruction in psychology to be tailored to school teachers and psychologists who work in the schools.

The most important work of this lifetime is raising, educating, and supporting our country’s children, and school psychologists are fully capable of meeting their academic, developmental, behavioral, and psychological needs. Moreover, as schools continue to be unfortunate sites of shootings, bullying and harassment, and in rare instances, suicides, school psychologists remain uniquely capable of responding to these crises and emergencies. They are specifically trained on how to handle crises in uncertain situations, conduct threat assessments, and de-escalate situations. However, even with the abundance of training that they have, school psychologists endure the misperception that their training is somehow less rigorous than that of their colleagues in clinical or counseling psychology.

School psychology students are less likely to secure APA-accredited doctoral internships, which, in part, is attributed to internship directors’ unwillingness to review applications from school psychology students. One potential reason for this unwillingness is the misperception that school psychology students lack preparation in counseling and mental health interventions. This is surprising, considering that the curriculum in clinical, counseling, and school psychology is more similar than it is different.

Furthermore, school psychology graduate students are not only trained to understand school systems and special education law, but they also gain knowledge in clinical and counseling psychology. School psychology graduate students learn about developmental psychopathology, mental disorders, counseling theories, and therapeutic interventions, which form a solid foundation in understanding human functioning.

For quite some time, schools, particularly those in rural areas, have grown accustomed to supporting the needs of students without school psychologists. This is risky territory given how high the stakes are. So how could this issue be solved? For now, the best approach is to encourage prospective applicants to clinical and counseling programs to apply to school psychology programs. If a qualified applicant is interested in working with children, supporting children’s social and emotional learning, being an advocate, and working with families, you are urged to consider this field!

#4840. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a new study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

They said their findings are important because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

The participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

However, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”

Shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi said genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”

#4839. How This Man Transformed His Body with 20-Minute Home Workouts and Minimal Equipment

After years of feeling “skinny fat,” Skye Mackintosh set himself a challenge.

Between work, family commitments, and a social life, finding time to exercise can feel like one of the biggest barriers to getting in shape.

Skye Mackintosh set out to prove that you don't need hours in the gym to transform your physique. Instead, he committed to just 20 minutes of exercise every day, documenting his progress over almost a year.

After 340 days, his transformation has attracted thousands of followers. Throughout the challenge, Mackintosh relied on simple home workouts using little more than his bodyweight, a kettlebell, and a handful of basic equipment. More recently, he added a weighted vest to keep challenging himself.

Mackintosh's motivation came after years of feeling unhappy with his physique.

“As a teenager I was naturally skinny,” he wrote on Instagram. ‘Then, as an adult, my age, eating habits, and lack of consistent exercise caught up to me. For 10 years I was ‘skinny fat.’”

Before beginning the challenge, he focused on improving his diet. After cutting out added sugar for a year, he lost 18 pounds. But the weight loss alone wasn't enough to make him feel the way he wanted, prompting him to start strength training at home.

“I cut out added sugar for a year and lost 18lbs,” he shared. “I felt better but not great. I knew that I needed to change and that accountability would help. So I started working out in my bedroom and posting it online. I was humbled and blown away that thousands rallied to support and keep me going. I put on about 8 pounds and made it to day 100.”

Another 100 days later, he'd gained roughly 18 pounds in total. While he felt stronger, he admitted: “I felt strong but didn't feel confident with how I was looking. The extra weight had me feeling a bit sluggish.”

Mackintosh's next goal was to reduce his body fat while holding on to the muscle he'd built. By Day 300, he weighed 3 pounds less than he had on Day 1, but looked considerably leaner and more muscular.

“I feel strong, athletic, and most importantly: happy. I learned to trust myself and the process,” said Mackintosh.

Mackintosh's transformation is a reminder that you don't need marathon gym sessions to make meaningful progress. Twenty minutes of strength training performed consistently can add up over time, particularly when paired with progressive overload and a supportive diet.

As his results show, the best training plan isn't necessarily the most complicated—it's the one you can stick to for the long term.

Kate is a fitness writer for Men’s Health UK where she contributes regular workouts, training tips and nutrition guides. She has a post graduate diploma in Sports Performance Nutrition and before joining Men’s Health she was a nutritionist, fitness writer and personal trainer with over 5k hours coaching on the gym floor. Kate has a keen interest in volunteering for animal shelters and when she isn’t lifting weights in her garden, she can be found walking her rescue dog.

#4838. The Art of Asking Questions

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

I recently got invited to a Halloween party where I knew only the hosts. People close to me think I am a major extrovert, so they may assume that going to a party filled with strangers would be easy-peasy for me.

But the truth is, I had to force myself to go. Quite honestly, I love deep, meaningful, one-on-one conversations—the deeper, the better—but small talk with new people? That’s a completely different story.

I decided to push myself outside my comfort zone to not only go to this party, but show up in a 1920s flapper costume. I definitely got an A+ for effort.

Although I had a good time, I must admit that, in some ways, the evening left me feeling empty.

Have you ever left a conversation knowing practically everything about another person’s life, only to realize that they learned almost nothing about yours?

They told you about their children, their travels, their work, their recent challenges. You listened. You asked questions. And you waited for a little curiosity to come your way.

Or perhaps they asked a question, but your answer merely provided a launching pad for another story about themselves.

“You’re a therapist?” “Yes,” I respond. And then I hear, “I once went to a therapist. I can’t believe what happened to me...”

What about, “What kind of therapy do you do?” or “What’s it like to work with couples teetering on divorce?” or "What do you do for fun when you're not working?"

When people share their own experiences, it can be a way of connecting. But there is a difference between offering something that deepens a conversation and taking it over.

As a therapist, I have spent nearly five decades asking questions. Yet you don’t need professional training to say, “What was that like for you?” or “Tell me more about that,” or “What happened next?”

Whatever happened to curiosity? Or giving people enough time to share their experiences without interruption?

Some people derive pleasure from talking about themselves. They like to entertain or impress. Others assume that if you have something to share, you will volunteer it.

But what they don’t realize is that being invited matters. It shows interest and caring.

And sometimes, we are simply so busy thinking about what we want to say next that we aren’t listening carefully enough to notice the opportunities to connect on a deeper level.

I don’t necessarily believe that people who dominate conversations are uncaring. In fact, I often assume that people who don’t ask questions probably grew up in homes where few meaningful questions were asked of them.

But regardless of the reasons that people prefer talking about themselves in conversation with you, there is loneliness in feeling unseen.

The art of asking questions begins with listening to the answer—and allowing it to influence what you ask next.

If a friend says that she is low on energy these days, instead of saying, “Yeah, me too,” we might ask if something unusual is going on in her life, if she has been taking good care of herself physically and emotionally, or what thoughts she has about why she feels depleted.

We don’t have to interrogate people. We can follow what they seem eager to share, respect what they prefer to keep private, and offer our own thoughts along the way. The goal is a genuine exchange, not a cross-examination.

Try noticing your next conversation. When someone finishes speaking, do you think about what you might ask to deepen your understanding of the speaker’s experience? Or do you find yourself immediately thinking how their story relates to you?

Do an experiment. Before you shift the conversation away from the speaker, consider asking one more question.

Being interesting has its place. So does being interested.

Too often, we underestimate how much the latter matters.

So, what do you think of my thoughts today? Inquiring minds want to know.

#4837. Toyota reveals five new lifted Woodland concepts, including the bZ electric SUV

Toyota introduced a new family of lifted, “adventure-ready” Woodland concepts based on the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, Crown Signia, and bZ electric SUV.

Toyota is the latest automaker to chase the highly profitable off-road market in the US, with plans to expand its “Woodland” lineup.

Although it already sells Woodland versions of the RAV4, Sienna, bZ, and most recently, the Grand Highlander, Toyota said the new family of concept vehicles is “designed for drivers who see adventure not as a destination, but a way of life.”

Toyota’s North American design studio, CALTY Design Research, designed the concepts to explore how some of its most popular nameplates can be used better on and off the road.

Each vehicle features Horizon Blue exterior paint, inspired by Toyota’s 1960s models, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona.

All new concepts also include an exclusive Woodland badge, plus a lift kit, large over-fenders, satin-black wheels, All-Terrain tires, two-tone paint on the roof and hood, a roof rack, and cross bars to top it off.

According to Toyota, the RAV4 Woodland Plug-In Hybrid and Sienna Woodland Concepts show how its “electrified and family-focused vehicles take on a more adventurous role.”

The electric Woodland bZ Concept “extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery electric future.” Meanwhile, the Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct models to the lineup, Toyota said.

The company didn’t reveal any powertrain specs or other details, but said the concepts show how capability can take many forms, including PHEV, hybrid, and battery electric.

Toyota’s new Woodland Concepts will be on display at the 2026 SEMA Show, starting on November 3.

To give you an idea, the 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower. That’s an extra 37 hp compared to the standard bZ with AWD.

And for a mere 10-15% reduction in efficiency, our beautiful American suburbanites can Look Butch as they drive about town. Hopefully Toyota offers a package that attaches a shovel and some jerry cans to complete the image.

The bZ Woodland also adds off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and the ability to tow up to 3,500 lbs.

Other rugged upgrades include All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

#4835. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4834. Are Pain Patients Denied Opioids Because of Addiction Fears?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Are patients with severe chronic pain being denied effective treatments because physicians fear prescribing opioids? Pain is one of the most common reasons adults seek medical care in the United States, with recent Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Health Interview Survey data indicating that the prevalence of chronic pain has risen to 24.3 percent of the adult population. Of those individuals, approximately 8.5 percent experience high-impact chronic pain, which severely limits daily life or work activities.

Severe chronic pain disrupts sleep, mobility, work, and family life. Yet some physicians fear causing addiction by prescribing opioids, even when other treatments have failed.

The opioid epidemic taught medicine painful lessons about indiscriminate prescribing. But have we gone too far in the opposite direction? Have we confused physical dependence with opioid use disorder (OUD), exaggerating addiction risks for patients taking prescribed medications appropriately? Patient complaints and new studies suggest we may have.

A 2026 study by Yarborough and colleagues examined 1,952 patients receiving long-term opioids through 10 U.S. health systems. Researchers followed participants for one year and assessed them using structured diagnostic interviews adapted for patients treated for pain.

Using pain-adjusted Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria, 1.54 percent developed moderate-to-severe OUD over one year, compared with 4.46 percent using unadjusted criteria. That's nearly a threefold difference in estimated addiction risk, depending on how OUD is diagnosed.

I have described this many times here, but patients chronically taking opioids develop a tolerance. They show withdrawal symptoms when opioid medication is reduced. These pharmacological adaptations are not addictions since the DSM-5 specifically excludes tolerance and withdrawal during appropriate medical treatment.

Taking additional medication because of intense or chronic pain needs evaluation, keeping the clinical context in mind. It may reflect misdiagnosis and inadequate pain analgesia. It can also be a sign of misuse or developing addiction. These are very different diagnoses.

A 2018 systematic review by Higgins and colleagues examined 12 studies involving more than 310,000 patients, with a pooled opioid dependence or abuse incidence of 4.7 percent.

A 2024 review by Kyla H. Thomas and University of Bristol Medical School colleagues included 148 studies involving more than 4.3 million patients with chronic noncancer pain. It estimated 9.3 percent for dependence and OUD combined, 29.6 percent for related symptoms, and 22 percent for aberrant drug-related behaviors.

The prevalence of OUD among patients already receiving opioids differs from the incidence of newly diagnosed OUD. Neither establishes lifetime addiction risk when treatment begins.

These data are concerning. However, problematic medication-taking behavior does not necessarily establish OUD.

In 2010, my anesthesiology pain clinic colleagues and I at the University of Florida (UF) published "Crossroads of Pain and Addiction" in Pain Medicine. Based on our clinic experiences, we argued that chronic pain and addiction regularly coexist. Physicians must assess and treat both, and not assume that restricting opioid prescriptions prevents addiction. Our multidisciplinary pain clinic experience showed us that what mattered were individual vulnerability, current and previous substance use disorders (SUDs), opioid selection, delivery, timing, and environment.

We distinguished between addiction and physiological dependence and called for integrated pain and addiction care. Pain specialists needed addiction training; addiction specialists needed greater expertise in pain management.

More than 15 years later, these lessons remain highly relevant. Reducing prescriptions without improving diagnosis, clinical training, and continuity of care is not comprehensive treatment.

My subsequent pain and addiction research with Washington University colleagues found patients receiving opioids for chronic pain frequently underestimated their own overdose risk. In a study of 190 chronic pain patients receiving higher-dose opioids, benzodiazepines, or both, 62.1 percent believed they had no overdose risk. More than half received benzodiazepines, yet fewer than half recognized the dangers of combining these medications.

In a related 2023 study, we compared these patients with 152 people with a documented OUD history. Only 19.1 percent of the OUD group perceived no overdose risk, compared with 62.1 percent of chronic pain patients.

These observational surveys identified an important gap between medical risks and patient perceptions. Patients do not have to be addicted to suffer an overdose. In fact, opioid-naïve or detoxified patients have a high risk of respiratory depression with opioid use. Naloxone education and access are essential for people taking opioids.

We should stop making these two mistakes: diagnosing addiction when there is only physical dependence, and overlooking overdose risks because patients are not addicted.

A 2025 report by Penn State’s Matthew Carrillo and colleagues studied 1,001 chronic pain patients, finding that more than half reported difficulty obtaining pain medication. Some patients reported seeking opioid pain medication from illicit sources, and nearly half contemplated suicide.

Another 2025 observational study, by Wei and colleagues, found that unrelieved pain among older adults prescribed opioids was associated with increased risks of OUD and overdose.

Untreated pain is not a successful addiction-prevention strategy. Public health analyses estimate chronic pain is a contributing or present factor in 8.8 to 10.2 percent of recorded suicide cases in the United States.

A 2026 study by Sarah Gutkind and colleagues at Weill Cornell Medicine surveyed chronic pain patients and physicians, examining perceived stigma around prescription opioids.

Physicians were much more likely than patients to anticipate stigma and unfair treatment by prescribing/using opioids. Nearly half of physicians (49.8 percent) anticipated negative judgments compared with 29.8 percent of patients.

This study measured perceived stigma, not actual prescribing decisions. Still, concerns about judgment may shape the environment where pain treatment decisions are made.

Both groups perceived slightly greater stigma associated with medical cannabis than prescription opioids. But more recent studies suggest that when cannabis and opioids are co-prescribed for pain, opioids are more often discontinued.

A 2017 CDC study found that approximately 6 percent of patients prescribed opioids for at least one day continued treatment a year later. But continued opioid use is not addiction. Prescription records alone cannot tell us who has an OUD, who benefits from treatment, and who develops problems.

The CDC's 2016 opioid prescribing guidelines were often applied too rigidly, sometimes beyond their intended scope. The CDC agreed and revised them in 2022.

It is more complicated, but our UF multidisciplinary pain program allowed us to evaluate the whole person. Physicians should evaluate pain, function, treatment response, and addiction risk, including previous SUDs, psychiatric illness, overdose history, and concurrent sedative use. Alternatives include non-opioid medications, physical therapy, rehabilitation, and psychological treatments.

Long-term opioids have uncertain benefits and significant risks, especially for many chronic pain conditions. Some patients do benefit; most others do not.

New research does not make opioids safer. It reminds us that physical dependence, misuse, and addiction are not the same diagnosis.

The good news is that medical pain treatment is evolving. In January 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Journavx (suzetrigine), a first-in-class, non-opioid analgesic—a new treatment for acute pain, without opioid-mediated respiratory depression or addiction risks.

Treatment should be individualized, with realistic goals, appropriate trials of newer alternatives, regular reassessment, and flexibility for patients who benefit from long-term opioid therapy.

The goal is not more or fewer opioids at any cost. It is better pain relief, more accurate addiction diagnosis, safer prescribing, and improved clinical outcomes.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

#4833. Tesla drops car referral rewards, now pays owners in FSD for referrals

Tesla has launched a new referral program in the US that pays owners in Full Self-Driving (Supervised) instead of rewarding car sales. A referred owner gets one free month of FSD, and the referrer gets a free month or a $99 Tesla Credit if that person starts paying.

At the same time, Tesla’s Refer and Earn terms no longer list any vehicle as a qualifying purchase for buyer or referrer rewards. Buy a Tesla with a friend’s code today and neither of you gets anything.

To share a link, you need to be paying for FSD (Supervised) monthly or own it outright from before Tesla stopped selling it, according to Tesla’s FSD referral support page. Owners who got FSD through a one-year grant can’t participate. The link lives under “Refer and Earn” in the Tesla app, version 4.62.0 or later.

The person on the other end has to own a registered Tesla with compatible hardware, can’t have paid for FSD in the past 12 months, and can’t have bought it outright. There’s also a catch for recent buyers: anyone who got a free FSD trial with a new car is locked out of referral links until 12 months after that trial ends.

The bigger change is buried in Tesla’s Refer and Earn page. Buyer benefits now apply to solar panels only. Referrer benefits cover solar, first demo drives (up to 30 over an account’s lifetime) and the new FSD referral.

Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck only show up under loyalty benefits, for existing owners buying another Tesla product. Model S and Model X aren’t listed at all.

Tesla didn’t announce the change. The page is stamped “Updated February 24, 2026,” so it’s unclear exactly when vehicles came off the list.

That’s quite a turn for a program that was always about moving cars. When Tesla brought the referral program back in August 2024, a buyer got $1,000 off a Model S, X, Y or 3, and the referrer got $500 in credit. Tesla has killed and revived the program several times over the past decade, but cars were always at the center of it. Not anymore.

That’s the exact metric in Elon Musk’s 2025 CEO Performance Award, which includes a milestone of 10 million active FSD subscriptions. It’s the reason Tesla started disclosing the number in January in the first place.

The free month a friend receives doesn’t count toward that total. A paid conversion does, and that’s precisely the event the new program pays for.

The only way I would ever pay for FSD is if Tesla covered full comprehensive insurance for my vehicle and accepted all liability. Otherwise, it's a gamble with my (and others') life.

That they seem to prioritize this sham service (Just call it Assisted Driving for honesty sake?) versus improving the cars or lowering prices, tells me enough not to look at Tesla for my next vehicle.

The recipient has to already own a Tesla, so the program doesn’t add a single car to the fleet. It’s built to mine the existing fleet for subscriptions. Tesla had sold about 8.9 million vehicles by the end of 2025, and only 1.74 million are paying for FSD, so there’s plenty of room. At Q3’s pace, we estimated 10 million subscriptions is still about eight years away.

So Tesla stopped paying for referrals that require selling a car, and started paying for the ones that move the number in Musk’s pay package. We think that tells you a lot about where the company’s priorities are right now.

#4832. This 61-Year-Old Is in the Shape of His Life—and Credits This Exercise with Transforming His Chest

Ricky Dietrich says the incline cable pullover has been a game changer.

A stronger chest isn't built through endless bench pressing and cable flys alone. Sometimes, adding a less obvious movement to your routine can provide a completely different stimulus.

At 61, Ricky Dietrich claims he's in the best shape of his life, and one exercise he credits with helping build his chest is the incline cable pullover.

“This is one of the only exercises I owe my lower chest growth to,” he says. “It keeps constant tension through the entire rep, lets me push close to failure safely, and has been one of the biggest contributors to building a fuller lower chest.”

While Dietrich describes it as a lower-chest exercise, pullovers aren't quite that simple. Depending on your setup and technique, both your chest and lats can contribute to the movement, with small adjustments changing where you feel the exercise most.

The incline cable pullover is a variation of the classic dumbbell pullover, a movement famously championed by Arnold Schwarzenegger and his Golden Era contemporaries.

Dietrich's version swaps the dumbbell for a cable machine and performs the movement on an incline bench. The cable keeps tension on the working muscles throughout more of the range of motion, rather than allowing the resistance to drop away at certain points.

Technique matters, particularly if you want to bias the chest rather than allowing your lats to dominate.

Dietrich recommends beginning with your arms overhead, keeping them relatively close together and maintaining a proud chest as you pull the cable forwards. Rather than continuing until your hands reach your hips, stop while your arms are still roughly 45 degrees from your torso, squeezing your pecs hard.

Allowing your elbows to flare and driving them further towards your sides can shift more of the work towards your lats. Using a lighter load should also make it easier to control the movement and concentrate on the muscles you're trying to target.

Think of the incline cable pullover as an accessory rather than a replacement for your presses and flys. But if your chest training has become stale, it could provide a useful new angle.
