#4830. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

#4829. Two Technologies That May Advance Psychiatric Knowledge

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

By Eugene Rubin, MD, Ph.D., and Charles Zorumski, MD

Two recent articles in JAMA Psychiatry examine technologies that will likely advance psychiatric research and lead to future treatments. Noah Philip, Mascha van’t Wout-Frank, and Amanda Arulpragasam review the potential of focused ultrasound neuromodulation (FUS). Peter Manza, Charles Lynch, Joshua Siegel, and Jacqueline Clauss discuss longitudinal precision functional mapping.

Psychiatric conditions are increasingly understood as abnormalities in specific brain circuits. Many brain circuits associated with psychiatric symptoms involve brain structures deep inside the brain—that is, those not near the skull and below the cerebral cortex. Currently used stimulation techniques such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcortical direct current stimulation (tDCS) have less influence on deep brain matter than on brain areas nearer the skull surface. Another experimental technique, deep brain stimulation, requires neurosurgical intervention and, therefore, is being developed to treat refractory psychiatric conditions.

FUS is a form of neuromodulation that can reach deep brain regions without the need for invasive procedures. Parameters of this neuromodulation technique can be adjusted to target specific brain structures and lead to reversible physiologic effects that influence the function of deep brain regions. The exact nature of the induced physiologic changes is still being elucidated, but the mechanism may involve “mechanical effects on neuronal membranes mediated through mechanosensitive ion channels, modulation of synaptic plasticity, and neurovascular coupling.” Early work suggests that such reversible changes have the potential to produce clinical improvement in a variety of psychiatric disorders. More research is required to demonstrate safety and efficacy of this technology, but this work is rapidly proceeding as summarized in a recent review article in Biological Psychiatry by Amanda Arulpragasam and colleagues. More information about this technique will be forthcoming over the next several years.

Several brain circuits have been identified that are involved in cognitive, motivational, attentional, and emotional functions. Defining the specific anatomic structures in these circuits has traditionally been obtained by averaging results from multiple individuals. However, the exact locations of brain regions involved in a specific circuit vary in each person. Recently, it has been shown that the precise location of circuits can be identified in single individuals, although doing so requires a major investment in imaging time. By mapping the function of an individual’s brain circuitry repeatedly over time using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and correlating this activity with changes in symptom severity, it should be possible to better understand the relationship between symptom presentation and neural activity in specific brain regions in individual patients. Such knowledge should allow development of therapeutic approaches targeting specific brain regions in an individual. This mapping technique is called longitudinal precision functional mapping, and methods for this approach to shorten scan times are advancing rapidly.

If FUS is approved for human use, it will most likely be utilized to help people with severe symptoms that are not responsive to less intensive approaches such as pharmacotherapies and psychotherapies. Will FUS be more effective and safer than other stimulation techniques such as TMS? The possibility exists.

In addition, longitudinal precision functional mapping may help identify specific brain structures that could be targeted in an individual by brain stimulation techniques such as FUS.

If symptoms can be substantially ameliorated by therapeutic approaches that target specific deep brain circuits, it is likely that psychosocial and psychotherapeutic interventions will assist an individual in returning to activities involving family, friends, and work.

Philip, N.S., van't Wout-Frank, M., & Arulpragasam, A.R. (2026). Focused ultrasound neuromodulation in psychiatry—promises and challenges. JAMA Psychiatry. 83(10):1080–1082.

Manza, P., Lynch, C.J., Siegel, J.S., & Clauss, J.A. (2026). Longitudinal precision functional mapping in psychiatry. JAMA Psychiatry. 83(10):999–1000.

Arulpragasam, A.R., Theyel, B., Barredo, J., Pouille, F., Gillotti, J.G., Greenberg, B.D., van't Wout-Frank, M., & Philip, N.S. (2026 Mar 6). Low-intensity focused ultrasound neuromodulation in psychiatric disorders: mechanisms, models, and missing links. Biol Psychiatry. doi: 10.1016/j.biopsych.2026.02.019. Online ahead of print.

#4828. The Bestselling Protein Powder on Amazon Is Also Our Budget-Friendly Pick

We’ve been using Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey for years. Here’s what you need to know.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THERE’S NEVER BEEN a better time to focus on your protein intake, with an arsenal of products ready to help you meet your macros. When tossing back chicken breast or sirloin isn't an option, protein powder is a valuable tool, especially when it comes to building lean muscle and promoting recovery. Unfortunately, most protein powders aren't cheap.

It's fair to be wary of budget options, especially if you use protein powder regularly. But there's an inexpensive protein powder that's an Amazon bestseller that's worth considering. It's called Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey, and we keep coming back to it. While it's not the cheapest protein powder you can find, the brand does a solid job balancing out nutritional needs and quality at a price tag most people can afford.

No protein powder is perfect, including this one. But with nearly 81,000 five-star reviews to back it up, plus an Informed Choice certification, you have to wonder if there's something to Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard. Two Men's Health editors put this powder to the test over several months, and have largely positive things to say about it. Keep these in mind before adding this protein powder to your cart.

The low price is what brings most people to the table for Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey. While price per serving varies depending on the size you buy, you're looking at $1.06 to $1.54 per serving, with more savings the larger the container you purchase.

By comparison, our best overall protein powder, Transparent Labs Grass-Fed Whey Protein Isolate, is $2 per serving. Should price be the main reason you choose a protein powder? Definitely not. But if you're able to get what you're looking for in an inexpensive powder, why wouldn't you go with it?

"The value is something to give props to," says MH Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. The brand is able to keep the cost down because this isn't a pure whey protein isolate, Thorp explains. Instead, it's a blend of whey protein isolate, whey protein concentrate, and hydrolyzed whey protein. Still, that delivers 24g of protein and 5.5g of BCAAs per serving.

Texture matters with protein powder, and some can lean toward a sandy or gritty feel. That usually means it won't blend as well in your shake or smoothie, which can make it tough to keep using a product. But Optimum Nutrition has a light texture that blends easily.

"It’s fluffy, not sandy, like some protein powders," says MH Deputy Editor Paul Kita. "That tells me it’s going to blend well and won’t sit heavy in my gut." Thorp also praises Optimum Nutrition's texture. "The powder itself is lighter than the majority of other protein powders, which is nice because it opens up your options for mixers," he says. (Powders with a gritty or sandy texture don't usually mix well with water or thinner liquids.)

SHOP OPTIMUM NUTRITION WHEY PROTEIN POWDER

Optimum Nutrition has an impressive lineup of 24 flavors, ranging from basic options like chocolate and vanilla to things like banana cream. There are 10 different chocolate flavor combinations alone, giving you plenty to choose from.

"I’m a huge fan of the chocolate flavor," Kita says. "It’s not too sweet—a major protein powder deal-breaker for me." Kita finds it blends equally well in berry, banana, or black cherry smoothies. Thorp says the milk chocolate taste is "light" and agrees it works well with a range of smoothies and mixers. "The taste isn't overpowering at all, which is nice as it allows you to build your taste from the other real foods you like," he says.

It doesn't hurt to remind everyone that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) doesn't really regulate supplements, including protein powder. As a result, what the label says doesn't always reflect what's inside the container. That makes third-party testing crucial. It verifies that you're actually getting what you think when you use a protein powder.

Optimum Nutrition is Informed-Choice Certified, which means it's regularly tested for unsafe and banned substances by LGC, an independent sports anti-doping lab. As a result, you can feel pretty solid reaching for this on a regular basis.

Thorp has been using Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey for years, including testing it more extensively over the past few months for this story. He regularly tried the powder blended into smoothies with peanut butter, banana, chia seeds, and coconut milk. He also had it occasionally mixed into whole milk.

Kita also tested the protein powder for months, blending it into smoothies with frozen fruit, chia seeds, and almond milk. During testing, MH editors took careful notes on elements like taste, texture, mixability, and value.

SHOP OPTIMUM NUTRITION WHEY PROTEIN POWDER

There is a trade-off to this powder's fluffy texture: It's not thick enough to mix with water. "For thicker protein powders, I like the ability to sometimes just mix water," Thorp says. "That isn't really an option with this one, which is one small detractor." (It did just fine in thicker consistency liquids like milk or smoothies, though.)

There's no outright harm when you have it in moderation, but it's worth noting that Optimum Nutrition relies on artificial sweeteners in its protein powder.

For most people, the blend of whey proteins isn't an issue. But if you have a sensitive stomach, it may be better to use a less dairy-heavy whey isolate instead.

If you like the idea of using whey protein and are OK with spending a little more, the Transparent Labs Grass-Fed Whey Protein Isolate is a MH favorite thanks to its clean ingredients, high protein content per serving, and wide range of flavor options.

For athletes, we dig Thorne Whey Protein Isolate. It's NSF-certified for professional athletes and blends well in water, milk, and smoothies.

There's an overwhelming number of protein powders to choose from out there. But if you want an inexpensive workhorse protein powder that'll help you meet your macros and actually contains what the label states, the Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey is worth your time.

#4827. The Correlation Between Sports and Suicide

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

The list of professional athletes who have killed themselves is long. It includes all-pro football players Junior Seau, Mike Webster, and Jim Tyrer; “Miracle on Ice” hockey star Mark Pavelich; Olympic beach volleyball medalist Mike Whitmarsh; Olympic freestyle skiing medalist Jeret Peterson; Olympic women’s cycling medalist Kelly Catlin; pro golfer Erica Blasberg; Cy Young Award winner Mike Flanagan; Yankees pitcher Hideki Irabu; and Angels pitcher Donnie Moore.

One reason why athletes have a high risk of suicide is that people who have enjoyed adulation and success throughout their young lives sometimes have a hard time adjusting when their playing days end. The roar of the crowd is gone, the adrenaline rush that accompanies top-level competition is no longer there, big paychecks most likely have ceased, locker room camaraderie is absent, and trainers and agents aren’t around to provide round-the-clock personal care. Most athletes who leave the game are still young by professional standards, whereas others in their 30s have begun to establish them­selves in long-term careers; athletes are just starting out and may not be prepared for life after sports.

According to one university researcher, 77 former Major League Baseball players have killed themselves. More than half were between their late 20s and late 40s, when their absence from the game was the most pronounced and future plans were uncertain, leading the researcher to recommend that MLB players receive counseling after they retire.[1]

Another factor is that many professional athletes leave the game with beat-up bodies. They were in peak physical shape when they first started playing, but overuse of joints and muscles plus injuries have taken a toll, mentally as well as physically. It’s hard to say goodbye to the limelight, but even harder sometimes to adjust to life afterward—chronic pain, decreased mobility, and—if they have suffered concussions—possible and permanent brain impairment.

In recent years, the results of studies on CTE—brain degeneration caused by repeated head trauma—have raised troubling concerns. At this time, there isn’t an accurate diagnostic test for CTE in living brains—it can only be found postmortem—but Chris Nowinski, a behavioral bio-scientist who played football in college, says that 99 percent of former NFL players whose brains have been examined posthumously have had CTE, and more than a few have died by suicide.[2]

Horse racing presents its own challenges. First and most obviously, it’s extremely dangerous. According to the president and CEO of the Jockey’s Guild, two jockeys die each year, on average, from racing, and 60 others are paralyzed. The concussions that jockeys get from falling off a horse at high speeds are as violent as the collisions of football players, and jockeys wear less protective gear. Add to this the challenge of maintaining a low weight, which results in eating disorders, plus frequent criticism from owners, trainers, and bettors, and it’s not surprising that jockeys suffer a variety of mental health issues. Three years ago, the horse racing world was stunned by the suicides of two jockeys. One of them was a friend of Mike Smith, who won the Triple Crown in 2018 at the age of 52 and is in the Racing Hall of Fame. Smith said that he knew other riders who killed themselves. “This is not all of a sudden just happening,” he said. “It’s been going on. You just never heard of it.”[3]

To date, only one female athlete has been diagnosed with CTE—a former Australian rules football player who played seven games in 2017, retired later that year, and killed herself in 2022 at age 28. Her family donated her brain to the Australian Sports Brain Bank, and the director there reported that he found “multiple CTE lesions.”[4] Here in the United States, two former World Cup stars, Brandi Chastain and Michelle Akers, have expressed public concern over memory-loss issues after they retired, and said that they will participate in a CTE study at Boston University.

Players and former players aren’t the only people at risk of suicide, however. Studies show that when a city’s most popular sports teams win a national championship, there is a temporary decline in the suicide rate. Conversely, after a loss, the rate goes up.

The U.S. men’s hockey team’s 1980 Olympic victory over the Soviet Union—the so-called “Miracle on Ice”—came at a time when the Iran hostage crisis had gone on for 111 days, and Russia’s invasion of Afghanistan was a month old. Millions of people in America had never seen a hockey game, didn’t know the rules or the names of any of the players, yet were glued to their TV sets and radios, cheering the home team to victory. It’s not surprising that the U.S. suicide rate was unusually low that day, February 22, 1980, compared with other February 22nds in the 20 years before and 20 years after.[5] (It may have been unusually high in the Soviet Union, although there are no data available to verify this.)

Suicide expert Thomas Joiner, who conducted that study, has conducted other studies that show a link between the success or failure of a sports team and suicide. For example, he found that fewer suicides occur on Sundays in America when the Super Bowl is played than on other Sundays during the year. Also, he determined that there is a correlation between the suicide rate and the national rankings of the football team at Florida State University, where Joiner is a tenured professor, and Ohio State University, which is a perennial football powerhouse. When the team was highly ranked, the suicide rate in the two cities—Gainesville and Columbus, respectively—was lower, Joiner found.[6]

Other studies support this. In one study of 30 metropolitan areas in the U.S. over 20 years, researchers noted that the suicide rate went down when the area’s pro team made the playoffs and went on to win a champion­ship.[7] Conversely, the defeat of a high-profile soccer team in England led to increased cases of self-poisoning, according to a different study.[8] In a third study, suicides of young men increased in Quebec when the Montreal Canadiens hockey team lost an early-round playoff series.[9]

People joke about “living and dying” with their favorite team, but the sense of belongingness that someone feels rooting for a team can be undone when that team loses and its season is over. It’s easy to say that no one should take sports so seriously, but as a fan myself, I’m aware of the lure.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

[1] Torre, Pablo S. “A Light in the Darkness,” Sports Illustrated, June 21, 2010.

[2] Nowinski, Chris. “Troubling Trend,” Sports Illustrated, July 16, 2018.

[3] Whyno, Stephen. “Weight Watching, Injury Dangers, Caustic Feedback Add to Mental Health Woes for Horseracing Jockeys,” Associated Press, May 23, 2023.

[4] ESPN News Services. “Heather Anderson Diagnosed with CTE in 1st Case for Female Athlete,” July 4, 2023.

[5] Joiner, Thomas. Why People Die by Suicide, 130-1.

[6] Joiner, Thomas. Why People Die by Suicide, 130.

[7] Fernquist, R.M. “An Aggregate Analysis of Professional Sports, Suicide, and Homicide Rates, 30 Metropolitan Area, 1971-1990,” Aggression and Violent Behavior, 2000, p. 329-341.

[8] Steels, M.D. “Deliberate Self-Poisoning—Nottingham Forest Football Club and F.A. Defeat,” Irish Journal of Psychological Medicine, 1994, p. 76-78.

[9] Trovato, F. “The Stanley Cup of Hockey and Suicide in Quebec, 1951-1992,” Social Forces, 1998, p. 105-126.

#4826. Winter’s Most Wanted: Tommy Hilfiger Holiday Picks for Every Occasion

From sharp knits to travel-ready extras, these are the pieces worth putting on your list.

The sweater that looked fine in October suddenly feels too thin, the jacket you reach for every day isn’t warm enough, and a weekend away calls for more than whatever you can squeeze into an overnight bag. Then there’s the rest of the season: office parties, cold walks across town, slow mornings at home, and the occasional trip out of town. Getting dressed for all of it takes a few reliable essentials.

Tommy Hilfiger has been building its take on American style since 1985, when the brand launched with a fresh spin on classic menswear. Its signature mix of preppy staples, sporty details, and relaxed ease has made it a year-round proposition, with pieces that move from everyday dressing to more seasonal needs. For winter, that means familiar wardrobe staples with a little extra warmth, practical layers for unpredictable weather, and accessories suited to life on the go. These six picks cover the season from the first cold snap to the last weekend getaway. Here’s what we’re putting on our fashion gift list.

A cable-knit sweater is a cold-weather staple, and Tommy Hilfiger’s take keeps the look classic. Made from combed cotton with a traditional cable pattern and ribbed trim, it’s an easy layer under a wool coat or a natural choice for a casual holiday gathering. Pair it with dark jeans or chinos for a straightforward winter look.

For trips, a jacket that barely takes up any room in your bag is always useful. Tommy Hilfiger’s lightweight puffer folds into its own interior zip pocket, making it easy to stash for a weekend away or keep on hand when the forecast is unpredictable. It has thermal insulation, a regular fit, and side pockets, so it’s a practical layer for travel and everyday errands alike.

A good winter evening often calls for staying in, and this sleep set makes a comfortable night at home feel a little more put together. This one pairs a simple T-shirt with plaid flannel pants, bringing a classic cold-weather pattern into the mix. It’s an easy gift for someone who appreciates a slow weekend morning as much as a cozy night in.

A warm beanie is one of winter’s most useful accessories, and this one gets an upgrade with a cotton-cashmere blend. The classic knit is an easy finishing touch for everything from a morning commute to a weekend walk. It’s also a practical gift that will see plenty of use once the temperature drops.

A card holder and keychain are the kind of everyday essentials that make an especially easy gift. Tommy Hilfiger’s leather set brings the two together in one package, with a polished finish that feels a step up from the usual stocking stuffer. It’s a useful pick for someone who likes to keep their daily carry simple.

A weekend away calls for a bag that can handle a change of clothes and a few extra essentials without looking like you’re heading to the gym. Tommy’s leather duffel brings a more polished feel to the overnight bag, making it a smart companion for a winter getaway or a quick trip home for the holidays.

#4825. What Kids Won't Tell Their Parents

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

November is a good month to be a child in the Gulf. The heat has broken, and families are outside in the evenings for the first time since spring. It is also the point in the school year when the novelty has worn off. Friendship groups have settled, and the first-term report cards are a few weeks away.

For many parents, this is when “How was school?” starts to get the same one-word answer every afternoon: "Fine."

Here in the Gulf, that answer can cover a lot. Our children attend demanding schools in a competitive environment. Their friendship groups shift every year as families arrive and leave, and many of them have been the new child more than once. They are navigating friendship politics and the pressure to do well, and much of it never comes up at home.

This is not unusual, and it is not a sign that something is wrong. Keeping some things private is a normal part of growing up. The more useful question is what leads children to open up.

Two influential studies by Kerr and Stattin (2000) examined how parents come to know about their children’s lives. The common assumption was that parents who ask more questions and keep closer track know more. Instead, the researchers found that parents’ knowledge came mostly from what their children chose to tell them. Spontaneous disclosure, rather than tracking or questioning, predicted how much parents knew, and it was linked to better adjustment in the children themselves.

We cannot question our way into our children’s inner lives. We can only make it more likely that they will let us in.

In our part of the world, there is an additional layer. In my research with Arab families, honor and reputation came up again and again as issues that mattered to young people and their parents, and they were not well captured by the Western measures of family conflict available to us (Rasmi, Daly, & Chuang, 2014). Children in our communities learn early that some things reflect on the whole family and that awareness makes them more careful about what they bring home.

Younger children often do not have the words yet. A 9-year-old who feels left out at school rarely says so. Instead, her parents hear about her stomach ache on a Sunday evening.

One finding from my own work has stayed with me. When we asked young Arab Canadians how they handled disagreements with their parents, the most common approach was to oblige (i.e., to go along with what their parents wanted). On the surface, this looked like the least conflict of all. However, we found, in interviews with emerging adults, that obliging took two distinct forms: Some young people genuinely deferred to their parents, whereas others said yes to their parents’ faces and then quietly did what they had planned anyway (Rasmi, Daly, & Chuang, 2014).

That second group is the one parents need to think about. A child who has learned that disagreement is not safe at home keeps disagreeing but stops telling you about it.

In a follow-up study, we interviewed young people about their relationships with their parents and found that the quality of the relationship shaped almost everything else (Rasmi, Chuang, & Hennig, 2017). Young people talked through their differences when the relationship was close, trusting, and marked by open communication. On the other hand, they withheld information to avoid conflict when they perceived the relationship to be distant or strictly hierarchical. In our quantitative research, a stronger parent–child relationship was also associated with less conflict at home (Rasmi, Chuang, & Hennig, 2015).

Smetana’s research points the same way. Adolescents disclose more to parents they experience as trusting and accepting. Children talk to the parents they feel safe with. That was true of the families I studied in Canada, and it is true of the families we see in Dubai.

Ask smaller questions. “How was your day?” invites one word. “Who did you sit with at lunch?” gives your child somewhere to start.

Talk side by side. Children share more when they are not being looked at directly, and this is the season for it. A walk on the beach after dinner gives you an hour with no screens and no eye contact. Bedtime works, too, when the lights are low.

Watch your reaction. Tilton-Weaver and colleagues (2010) found that when children met negative reactions after sharing something, they shared less afterward. Our response to the lost hoodie tells our children how we will respond to the bigger things.

Make disagreement safe. If your child can tell you they disagree and the conversation stays respectful, they are far more likely to tell you what is actually going on. You can hold your position and still let them voice theirs.

Let silence do some work. Children often circle a difficult topic before they land on it, and if we jump in too soon, they tend to retreat.

Notice what their body is saying. Stomach aches with no medical explanation can be a sign of something unsaid. So can a change in sleep or pulling away from things they used to enjoy. Several together, or any lasting more than a couple of weeks, are worth a gentle conversation and, if needed, a professional.

A child who keeps some things private while otherwise seeming like themselves is doing something healthy. A child who becomes withdrawn or unlike themselves alongside the silence may need more support. The goal is not to know everything, but to be the person your child comes to when it matters.

My colleagues Natalie Maaitah and Valen Valentine and I discussed this on a recent episode of our podcast, Thrive With Us. One idea stayed with me: Connection has to come before correction. Our children only tell us when they have learned that we are safe to tell.

November 20 is World Children’s Day, and its theme, in one form or another, is always listening to children. The cooler months give us more time together than any other part of the year. Some of it can go to smaller questions and to listening to the answers.

Kerr, M., & Stattin, H. (2000). What parents know, how they know it, and several forms of adolescent adjustment: Further support for a reinterpretation of monitoring. Developmental Psychology, 36(3), 366–380. DOI: 10.1037/0012-1649.36.3.366

Rasmi, S., Chuang, S. S., & Hennig, K. (2015). The acculturation gap-distress model: Extensions and application to Arab Canadian families. Cultural Diversity and Ethnic Minority Psychology, 21(4), 630–642. DOI: 10.1037/cdp0000014

Rasmi, S., Chuang, S. S., & Hennig, K. (2017). Seeing eye to eye in Arab Canadian families: Emerging adult perspectives. Journal of Adolescent Research, 32(3), 263–290. DOI: 10.1177/0743558416630814

Rasmi, S., Daly, T. M., & Chuang, S. S. (2014). Intergenerational conflict management in immigrant Arab Canadian families. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 45(7), 1124–1144. DOI: 10.1177/0022022114532358

Smetana, J. G., Metzger, A., Gettman, D. C., & Campione-Barr, N. (2006). Disclosure and secrecy in adolescent–parent relationships. Child Development, 77(1), 201–217. DOI: 10.1111/j.1467-8624.2006.00865.x

Smetana, J. G., Villalobos, M., Tasopoulos-Chan, M., Gettman, D. C., & Campione-Barr, N. (2009). Early and middle adolescents’ disclosure to parents about activities in different domains. Journal of Adolescence, 32(3), 693–713. DOI: 10.1016/j.adolescence.2008.06.010

Stattin, H., & Kerr, M. (2000). Parental monitoring: A reinterpretation. Child Development, 71(4), 1072–1085. DOI: 10.1111/1467-8624.00210

Tilton-Weaver, L., Kerr, M., Pakalniskeine, V., Tokic, A., Salihovic, S., & Stattin, H. (2010). Open up or close down: How do parental reactions affect youth information management? Journal of Adolescence, 33(2), 333–346. DOI: 10.1016/j.adolescence.2009.07.011

#4824. BYD reveals a flashy new feature on its upcoming luxury EV

BYD is moving upmarket with its new flagship EV, featuring suicide doors, a gemstone grille, and possibly solid-state batteries.

Yangwang is like BMW’s Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Maybach, sitting at the very top of BYD’s brand hierarchy.

The ultra-luxury brand offers BYD’s most high-end and technically advanced vehicles, including the U7 sedan, the U8, a hardcore off-road SUV, and the U9, an electric supercar.

Yangwang vehicles have previously debuted with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including its quad-motor e4 platform (delivering over 1,300 hp), its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its DiSus-X intelligent body control system.

Its next model will push further into the elite segment. After BYD revealed the name of its new flagship executive sedan earlier this week, the Yangwang Altior, the company has released several new details ahead of its official debut.

Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing confirmed on Friday that the new Yangwang Altior will feature suicide doors, a first for a BYD model.

The new door design swings open nearly 90 degrees, Hu said, creating a dramatic, wide-open entrance.

Hu also posted a preview of the vehicle’s front fascia, complete with a dot-matrix Gemstrone grille and crystal-inspired headlights.

BYD has not confirmed many details, but the ultra-luxury sedan is expected to be about 5,500 mm (216″) in length.

Images of the disguised vehicle released last month show a similar shape and size to the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom.

HU said last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China.

BYD has not revealed an official date, but according to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD aims to unveil the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5.

The Yangwang Altrio will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said.

In one image, the vehicle was charging at a BYD Flash Charge station, suggesting it will use its Blade Battery 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology.

There are companies showcasing flying cars designed specifically for circus-style shows, while others are launching solid-state batteries that can recharge in five minutes.

I find myself wondering—though perhaps not too deeply—which of these technologies will secure the largest customer base and generate the greatest returns for shareholders.

Outside of the suicide doors, rumors suggest the flagship model will be BYD’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries. Executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with Carwow.es last month that BYD’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027.

The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000.

Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The extended U8L, on the other hand, is the brand’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

#4823. Want to Get Closer With Your Spouse? Take on a Wife Carrying Competition.

One couple‘s experience taking on a race that demands they shoulder each others’ burdens—literally.

DANNY AND KATIE Young are both active, but they’re not exactly the type of couple that stakes out dates on their calendar for the next Hyrox doubles race. Over the last few years, however, both went through separate fitness journeys. So on Christmas Day 2025 when Danny's older brother, Dylan, asked if they had heard of a wild event called wife carrying, they felt ready to take on a new challenge together.

Danny and Katie watched YouTube clips of the North American Wife Carrying Championship, an annual race held every October at the Sunday River Resort in Newry, Maine. It’s exactly what the name implies: a 278-yard race where husbands carry their wives on their backs. This is not the only one of its kind—similar events are staged around the globe and there’s a world championship in Finland—and competition isn’t limited to only married or man-woman couples. The Youngs scrolled through videos of couples running a steep obstacle course, jumping hurdles and sloshing through mud pits all while struggling to stay upright to the finish. The Youngs decided they wanted to take on the event in the coming year.

“One, because it’s so silly and ridiculous,” Katie tells Men’s Health. “Two, we used to live in Boston and we wanted to get back up to New England. The competition (held October 10 this year) was right around our 16th wedding anniversary, so we figured, what better way to celebrate?”

“We are seize the moment people–even if the moment is 10 months in advance,” Danny adds. “Signing up for the competition also felt like a natural celebratory culmination of what we’d done in the last year. We felt like: this is just the sort of thing we’ve been getting ready for. Let’s go do that, to applaud a really cool year of physical and health transformation.”

DANNY AND KATIE met when they were 14 years old, dated in high school, and got married shortly after graduating college. Now 38, they live on a hobby homestead outside of Asheville, NC. Their day jobs (Danny works as a manager at Trader Joe’s, Katie is a clinical supervisor for a community mental health clinic) and taking care of their daughter, Opal, and their small farm leaves little time for traditional training.

But Katie and Danny have navigated the challenges that come with maintaining fitness through both the busy schedules of everyday life and unexpected circumstances. In August of 2023, Katie had ankle surgery and was non-weight bearing for 14 weeks. She gained more than 100 pounds, which was difficult to manage on her 5’3’’ frame. By Thanksgiving of 2023, she started walking with a crutch, but she wasn’t able to return to her workouts (mostly hot yoga) until the summer of 2024. She loves power flows, hot HIIT classes, and hot lifts. “If it’s not over 100 degrees, I’m not interested,” Katie says. “I like that it’s balance, strength, and there’s a cardio element at times.” Twice a week turned to four times a week and then six; by the summer of 2026, she had lost 120 pounds.

Danny had been a CrossFit devotee in his 20s. His job at Trader Joe’s is very physical, picking up and carrying 20 to 50 pound boxes throughout the day. He had abandoned his gym habit in his late 20s; by 30, he struggled with back problems. He returned to the gym three years ago, alternating between calisthenics and foundational compound lifts. He trained twice a week, then three times, then every day. He, too, spent the last year transforming his body from a “dad bod” to one chiseled with muscles—and in top shape, stands at 6’3” and weighs 185 pounds.

But in June of this year, Danny injured his back during a deadlift session. He didn’t lift any weights for the rest of the summer. The couple were still committed to take on the wife carrying contest—but they needed to find a new way to train. They leaned on their active lifestyle on the homestead. They keep four goats, and Katie found that carrying two five-gallon buckets of water up and down the farm’s hills several times a week increased her strength. Katie often picked up one of the 80-pound goats to “escort her out of my garden, where she wants to eat my pumpkins.”

When Danny carried the buckets, he’d sometimes throw Katie on his back. He also carried her around the house and up and down the hills near the farm. They discussed which carry style might work best for them, trying piggyback, upside-down, and other methods. They never attempted a full 278-yard training run, instead opting for spontaneous moments of carrying when circumstances allowed.

“I really like the dual challenge of it, which appeals to both of us,” Danny says. “It’s like a test of a relationship alongside a physical feat. Silly, physical antics are part of our love language.”

RACE MORNING IN Newry, Maine brought clear, blue skies and strong winds. Almost five dozen couples warmed up by jogging up and down the rolling hills of the Sunday River Ski Resort ski slope, navigating sections of the 278-yard course and attempting the log hurdle in the carry position. That’s one of the two dry obstacles on the course; the other is a sand trap.

Danny and Katie watched other couples warming up and did some light stretching. Danny pumped out several sets of pushups as they waited. Hundreds of spectators lined the course.

“The community element seemed really fun,” Katie says afterward. “I can see why a lot of people watch it every year, or why people participate every year.” They met a couple who’d traveled from Utah to compete. Another pair had participated every year for the last 25, while others were in their 60s.

An M.C. announced each set of couples, who competed against one another in rounds of two and for time; the fastest two teams from the qualifying rounds would compete head-to-head in a final heat to determine the winner. A record 58 couples had signed up to compete.

Finally, it was their turn. Katie and Danny wished good luck to their co-competitors, and after several false starts as the MC adjusted his mic, the couples took off. Danny jogged as Katie held on to him utilizing a variation of the popular “Estonian carry,” where she was positioned upside-down, facing his back, using her arms to grip her own legs, which were wrapped over his shoulders like a yolk. The strength and balance she’d built through yoga showed as she held steady, despite Danny’s wobbles on the uneven terrain. She relied on core strength primarily, but also her arms and inner thighs to stay in position.

“It turns out that holding on to your own legs like an upside down human backpack while your partner runs uphill, clambers over a log hurdle, and wades through mud is much harder than it looks,” Katie says. “You’ve got to crunch up as tight as you can, squeeze your legs around your partner, wrap your arms into your own legs, and brace your core; all the while feeling your blood rushing to your head. I think the only reason I was able to do it is from the strength, endurance, and flexibility I’ve gained from my hot yoga practice. Plus, if you can tolerate exercising in a 105 degree room, what’s a little bit of mud?”

The pair didn’t talk much during the race itself. “Most of the race, the noise I was making was something along the lines of, ‘this is so much harder than I thought it was gonna be,’” Danny recalls.

Katie felt the early section had gone well, even though she admittedly couldn’t see anything but the landscape passing below her. “And then, all of a sudden, I can see the ground is moving a lot slower, and Danny's panting and saying how hard it is,” she says.

Still, they kept moving, navigating a steep uphill and then descending toward the mud pit, the course’s final challenge also known as the “Widow-Maker.” Katie had photographed the mud pit prior to the race and texted her friends with the caption, “My fate.”

Danny stepped into the mud hole, navigating the first big step downward. He wobbled. Katie, sensing his unsteadiness, didn’t want to be dropped on her neck and head. “So I abandoned ship,” she says. She threw herself into the cold, wet mud, which filled her mouth and covered her eyes and nose. “It was a pretty solid belly flop,” she added. The muddy water coated her body, officially making the Youngs the first full “mud drop” out of the 30-plus couples that had competed up to that point.

“As I felt her coming off of my back, I thought, ‘where is she going?’” Danny adds afterward.

Katie stood up, wet and laughing so hard she needed a moment to steady herself. The plan had been for Katie to carry Danny across the finish line–but after they cleared the mud pit and stepped onto dry land, he was so wet and she was laughing so hard, she couldn't quite grip him. She jumped onto him, piggy-back, as they emerged from the mud pit and jogged the final yards to the finish line. Just before crossing, she hopped off his back and picked him up, carrying Danny across the finish, laughing as the crowd cheered.

The winning couple was celebrating their 10th anniversary, and their children joined them in crossing the finish line. Most of the competitors stayed through the full two-hour event, as did the spectators, watching the award ceremony and cheering for the various additional contests (best dressed couple and other superlatives.) The winning couple received the wife's weight in beer and five times her weight in cash. Volunteers handed out beers to the entrants. Katie changed out of her wet clothes before they joined his parents, Dylan and his wife, Kristen, and Katie and Danny’s 8-year-old daughter, Opal.

In carrying Danny across the finish, Katie wanted to reinforce what Opal had learned: “Mommy and Daddy are both strong and capable, and there’s no difference,” Katie says.

OVERALL, THE BIGGEST takeaway from the race had little to do with their time or the physical challenge that came with hauling one another across the course. Their relationship, they say, has always been strong—and attempting a fun, unique competition reinforced the tenets of their partnership: fun, laughter, strength, and supporting each other.

Danny suggested they enter again next year, “which I’m definitely up for, competition-wise,” Katie says. “I want to do many ridiculous competitions with you,” Danny adds. “Our relationship quality has been great, and this added another fun adventure.”

After the race, Danny considered how he might approach training for their next attempt. “If we were to run it back, I would definitely add hill sprints to my routine,” he says. “I should have prepared for the fact that the race is very short and very intense. Interval sprints and sled pushing would have been more aligned with the demands of the competition.”

But nothing, in his opinion, is better than replicating the real challenge of the event: carrying a partner and working together. “Spend as much time as possible with your wife on your back,” he says. “It's kooky and fun, and there's nothing else that quite mimics the awkwardness of two spouses becoming one athlete.”
